speechtext: Mr. Speaker, on Friday last I asked the Minister of Trade and Commerce whether a company by the name of Crossroads Marine Disposal Corporation of Boston was manufacturing at Nanaimo, British Columbia, containers for the disposal of atomic wastes, and the minister said he would look into the matter. speakerposition: Minister of Trade and Commerce; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: INQUIRY AS TO DISPOSAL OF U.S. ATOMIC WASTES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have found on investigation that a firm known as International Anti-Radiation Limited was set up in
[Mr. Badanai.)
Nanaimo, British Columbia, last year to manufacture spherical containers of high density concrete, reinforcing steel, dense glass, lead and polyethylene, in which radioactive wastes might be disposed of to the sea. This company, according to press reports, has signed a contract with a United States firm, licensed to dispose of low level United States radioactive wastes, for the use of these containers in its disposal operations.
The company has not been authorized by the atomic energy control board of Canada to receive or dispose of radioactive wastes in Canada or in the waters adjacent to Canada. Since no permit is required for the construction of containers provided radioactive materials are not placed therein, the company's construction activities are not affected, but the board has not approved the use of these containers for the disposal of radioactive wastes from Canada. It has advised the company that the suitability of the containers could be considered only in connection with an application to dispose of specific wastes. Similar arrangements are in effect in the United States but, so far as the board is aware, the atomic energy commission has not approved the use of these vessels for the disposal of United States radioactive wastes.
The subject is one of importance from the standpoint of protection for the public. Interested members might refer to the report of the committee on research which was made to the house some time ago. They will find there, in the statement made by the president of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, some reference to the care that is taken with regard to radioactive wastes, and it is interesting to note that the safety record of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited is very good indeed. No lost time injury has occurred in 15 years in the operations of Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, and this has been due largely to the supervision and control exercised by the radiation hazards control branch and the co-operation it receives from operating personnel throughout the project.

United Nations Forces in Congo
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think I should commence by placing on record the two resolutions that were passed by the United Nations security council, so the entire transaction which has made necessary the action now being taken will be before members of the house.
On the 13th July a resolution introduced by Tunisia was passed which reads:
The security council,
Considering the report of the secretary general on a request for United Nations action in relation to the Republic of the Congo,
Considering the request for military assistance addressed to the secretary general by the president and the prime minister of the Republic of the Congo (document S/4382),
Calls upon the government of Belgium to withdraw their troops from the territory of the Republic of the Congo;
Decides to authorize the secretary general to take the necessary steps, in consultation with the government of the Republic of the Congo, to provide the government with such military assistance as may be necessary, until, through the efforts of the Congolese government with the technical assistance of the United Nations, the national security forces may be able, in the opinion of the government, to meet fully their tasks;
Requests the secretary general to report to the security council as appropriate.
Then there was a revised draft resolution on the 22nd July, sponsored by Ceylon and Tunisia, which in part read as follows:
The security council,
Having considered the first report by the secretary general on the implementation of security council resolution S/4387 of 14 July 1960 (document S/4389),
Appreciating the work of the secretary general and the support so readily and so speedily given to him by all member states invited by him to give assistance,
Noting that as stated by the secretary general the arrival of the troops of the United Nations force in Leopoldville has already had a salutary effect,
Recognizing that an urgent need still exists to continue and to increase such efforts,
Considering that the complete restoration of law and order in the Republic of the Congo would effectively contribute to the maintenance of international peace and security,
Recognizing that the security council recommended the admission of the Republic of the Congo to membership in the United Nations as a unit,
Calls upon the government of Belgium to implement speedily the council resolution of 14 July 1960, on the withdrawal of their troops and authorizes the secretary general to take all necessary action to this effect;
Requests all states to refrain from any action which might tend to impede the restoration of law and order and the exercise by the government of Congo of its authority and also to refrain from any action which might undermine the territorial integrity and the political independence of the Republic of the Congo;
Commends the secretary general for the prompt action he has taken to carry out resolution S/4387 of the security council and his first report;
Invites the specialized agencies of the United Nations to render to the secretary general such assistance as he may require;


Requests the secretary general to report further to the security council as appropriate.
Those are the two resolutions upon which action is now invited and the approval of parliament asked. The constitutional position in this regard was set forth by the former prime minister, Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent, on November 20, 1956, when an order in council was passed which authorized the maintenance on active service of not more than 2,500 officers and men as part or in immediate support of the United Nations emergency forces in the Middle East.
A special session of the house was called and the order in council was duly tabled, at which time the then prime minister stated that it has always been the constitutional requirement and the constitutional practice that the government has to take the responsibility of making a decision, and then puts itself in the hands of parliament so that parliament may determine whether it will provide the funds to implement that decision, or whether it will refuse to provide the funds and get another government to carry out the policies that parliament wants to have carried out.
That has always been the position. That will always be the position, so long as this party has the responsibility for public affairs in this country. A supplementary $1 item in the estimates was debated and approved, without a vote being taken, on November 29.

speechtext: I wonder if the Prime Minister could give us the Hansard page reference he has just mentioned?

subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN FORCES IN CURRENT OPERATIONS
speechtext:
I have the copies of Hansard here. I thought I would simply summarize, and if there are any questions they can always be checked in Hansard and I will refer to the specific pages if required.
Today I had the opportunity of discussing something of the situation in the Congo with Air Commodore Carpenter of the R.C.A.F., who returned yesterday from the Congo. He was in charge of the air lift there, and those of other nations who saw something of the work he has done have given him high commendation.
He pointed out the situation as he saw it there in a way that could not be understood by simply reading the records and statements from those in the area. The views he expressed indicated something of the situation in that country. It is a vast country, situated on the equator, depending in the main on waterways, 1,000 miles on the Congo river and some 4,000 other waterway miles. Its communications generally are based on those waterways.
When independence came at the end of June the political and business administration

ceased to exist. Those Belgians with experience withdrew, and the result was that there was uncertainty in all parts of that country. With the withdrawal of the Belgian administration, with businessmen leaving and with other Belgians immediately departing from the country, there was brought about a situation which became difficult for the people of that country.
In saying that it is no criticism whatever of the action taken by the Belgian government or by Belgian nationalists. The Congo had achieved its independence. It had an administration to take over. But the difficulty apparently was this, that there was not that training and experience which is so necessary for administrators to have when suddenly propelled into a position of national responsibility. With the businessmen leaving, the result was that unemployment mounted and food in general became very scarce; for although the Congo supplies 97 per cent of all the food consumed in the country, no one had the money to make purchases. A dangerous situation resulting from hunger was the consequence.
In these circumstances I think I should also place before the house discussions which I had on Saturday with the prime minister of the Congo. He said he came to Canada because in the thinking of the people of his country Canada occupied a position of independence, coupled with a reputation for coming to the assistance of other nations with plans without strings attached.
Following his visit he made certain statements to the press in an interview, and I should like to make very clear the events which took place. He did not ask for any aid or assistance on the part of Canada directly or in any way outside the ambit of the United Nations in joint action. He indicated that he felt that in view of the bilingual nature of our country and the need for having French speaking technicians, Canada, he hoped, would provide a reservoir for the supply of needed agriculturists, teachers, doctors, nurses, lawyers, radio technicians, information and administrative officers and the like. He wanted a list, if he could secure one, of Canadians who might be available to go to the Congo in the event that financial arrangements to that end were made by the Congo government with the individuals in question.
I stated that we would communicate with universities, the national research council and professional bodies to the end that the needs of the Congo, would be made known to them, and he emphasized that any arrangements made would of course be made directly by representatives of his government. He further stated that he would like
United. Nations Forces in Congo Canada to participate in an investment program in his country, and I frankly told him that Canada, a country in a stage of great development, was herself in need of capital and that in this regard I did not expect that his hopes would be attained.
Also on Saturday I met with some Canadian missionaries who had just returned from the Congo. They were representatives of the Baptist and Mennonite faiths, and were brought to North America by airlift some ten days or two weeks ago. They informed me that while there was a feeling of antagonism against the whites in general, at no time had they been directly or physically interfered with; and I think it is proper to say that among all the missionary representatives of Catholic and Protestant denominations and faiths from Canada, none has been subjected to personal physical violence.
However, the interesting reaction of these people and the reason they came to Ottawa was that they felt that at the earliest possible date they should return to their responsibilities and fields of service. They felt that the missionaries of the various faiths and religious denominations in Canada would want to return there as soon as a reasonable degree of order had been re-established. They pointed out what is known to all of us, that wherever there is anarchy, chaos or economic dislocation there is a field for communist operations. They spoke in the highest terms of the treatment they had received. They also indicated the need of action being taken by the nations of the world to assure that the conditions existing in that country, wealthy but unfortunate in so far as civil disorder is concerned, should receive the attention of all of us.
In that regard it is obvious that the U.S.S.R. is using the situation prevalent in that country to assure that those conditions shall be magnified. Indeed, in the last few weeks the attitude of the U.S.S.R., particularly since early in May, has been one of aggressive and continuing threats. Only on Friday Tass, the official Soviet news agency, carried a government statement to the effect that it had become clear that "the aggressors in the Congo were acting with the encouragement of all the colonial North Atlantic treaty powers." This was a continuation of Premier Khrushchev's earlier view expressed on July 15, in which he referred to imperialist aggression in the Congo. Finally it was stated that Russia was ready to consider giving the Congo extensive economic assistance and "will not shrink from taking decisive measures to rebuff the aggressors who, as it has become quite clear, are acting with the encouragement of all the colonist powers of NATO."

United Nations Forces in Congo
That statement is hardly in keeping with the fact that the U.S.S.R. as a member of the security council must have voted for, or given its support to, the resolutions of the security council which I outlined at the beginning of my remarks. Indeed, on July 21 Mr. Khrushchev threatened to send troops to the Congo, although the Soviet representative in the United Nations security council voted for or supported the decision that no troops of major powers should be included in the international force.
The course of action taken by the U.S.S.R. in the past several weeks in the Congo incident is a continuance of the belligerent and even blatant attitude now being taken in many parts of the world by that country. It is of interest, too, that while Prime Minister Lumumba when he was in Washington refused to meet with the charge d'affaires of the Soviet embassy there, while he was in Ottawa he met with the ambassador of the U.S.S.R.
I repeat in summary what I have said, namely that the need of action being taken to restore equilibrium in the Congo is underlined by the fact that the U.S.S.R. has been making the threats to which I have referred. Indeed, in addition that country has endeavoured to supply foodstuffs directly to the Congo without going through the United Nations organization. All this if successful, could not but have an adverse effect on the strength, the authority and the responsibility of the United Nations.
During the years Canadians have advocated the need of an international force under the control of the United Nations to be available whenever required. I looked up some of the debates in parliament, and I am simply going to refer to them so as to make clear to hon. members the nature of the particular discussions which took place in this regard.
I spoke in this house on October 19, 1945 on the United Nations agreement which was then before us for consideration, and I said this, as reported at page 1308:
I know this charter will be approved, and, I hope unanimously, by parliament, but approval will be only lip service to its idealistic principles unless parliament faces the realistic problem of assuring not only by words but by pledges that Canada will contribute to and make available to the security council the necessary armed forces, assistance and facilities including the rights of unhampered international air passage across Canada and the use of her airports for the maintenance of international peace and security.
Then again, prior to the United Nations meeting in April, 1945, at San Francisco, I said speaking on the conference, as reported at page 163 of Hansard of March 23 of that year:

Are we going to incorporate a further provision whereby we in Canada shall determine not only the number of men we will supply and the nature of other support we may give, but in addition stipulate that the men we mobilize for an international force shall not be used beyond the confines of Canada? The Prime Minister finally used these words:
"As they stand, the acceptance of the proposals would in no way commit Canada to send forces beyond Canadian territory at the call of the security council. If any such commitment were sought, it would be embodied in a later agreement freely negotiated by the government of Canada, and coming into effect only after it had been approved by parliament."
With that statement I am not in disagreement in so far as it requires that this agreement, like any other of the kind, under the proposals, must be presented to parliament. But what is serious about that statement is that either unintentionally or designedly, page 26 of Hansard, on which the Prime Minister's remarks are reported, makes for controversy in this country at a time when there should be a united front. Surely one of the outstanding lessons we learned in the failure of the league of nations was that when the member nations of the league had the right to determine the degree of their obligation the league ended as an instrument to prevent war.
Then at page 164 I said:
The warning of 1919 comes back in 1945. The league of nations failed because it never had the power or strength of a real league. It failed because it lacked the united responsibility of all member nations to keep the peace; because it reserved to any and all of them the right to decide if and when and where they would co-operate to assure peace.
And a little later:
If we take away from our responsibility to contribute our part everywhere in the world we add to the probability that eventual impotence will come to the security council, for other nations may well follow our lead in this regard.
After referring to the fact that the one great contribution Canada could make in the building of a new world free from war would be to make available to the United Nations the strategic airports given to us by nature, I went on to say, as reported at page 165 of Hansard of March 23, 1945:
In that way we can do our part toward rendering available posts from which great international forces will be able to move in order to prevent aggression, not only within the confines of Canada but everywhere in the world where duty calls and parliament allows.
Our view at all times was that an international force available anywhere in the world was the one means whereby the high idealism inherent in the United Nations organization would become effective in the interests of world peace.
In addition, I think I should also refer to the discussion which took place in this house on January 31, 1956. At page 723 of Hansard of that date I set forth the views that had been expressed on earlier occasions. On that occasion the house was discussing the situation in the Middle East. I said that as far

as I could see the only immediate hope was to set up an international force to protect and assure the boundaries. I went on to say:
I suggest to my hon. friend who interrupted that one of the things he can do, with his influence in the United Nations, is to see to it that something in the nature of an international force is established to the end that this dangerous situation shall be obliterated. If it is not, and war breaks out, we shall have war all over the world-
I simply point out these instances in the past, beginning in March of 1945, to indicate that throughout that period of time the Conservative party took a strong stand on behalf of an international force.
An international force has now been set up to meet the delicate if not indeed the frightening situation in the Congo. I say that because unless a degree of order is established there, what is taking place in the Congo may, in the nature of things, be expected to expand. There will be a total of 12,140 in this international force consisting of 14 battalions and 5 companies representing nine countries: Ethiopia, Ghana, Guinea, Liberia, the Mali federation (Senegal and Sudan), Morocco, Tunisia. Haiti and Burma may also contribute. Ireland has already sent its force, one battalion, and Sweden has transferred 635 persons from the Gaza area. In addition to these there are military advisers from Canada, New Zealand, Norway, Sweden, Italy and Denmark.
I should pay the tribute of Canadians to the outstanding work done by all who have gone to the Congo, to the advance party of officers, and in particular Colonel Jean Ber-thiaume, chief of staff to Major General Von Horne, United Nations commander. Colonel Berthiaume is in charge of getting in troops and of deployment, and has earned the commendation of all who are contributing to the force. As I said earlier, the airlift has been in charge of Air Commodore Fred Carpenter, R.C.A.F., who has also made an outstanding contribution that has won widespread commendation.
What have we done? What has been Canada's contribution? I simply outline it for the record without going into particulars. Following the initial request the government authorized the secondment of five Canadian officers who volunteered from the United Nations truce supervisory organization in Palestine. Three of the five are now in Leopoldville. When it was reported that there was the risk of a food shortage the government decided to provide pork and dried powdered milk to which reference has already been made. These supplies were airlifted by R.C.A.F. North Star aircraft.
79951-0-463
United Nations Forces in Congo
The secretary general asked for the secondment of certain specialized personnel, including five Canadian officers serving with national contingents of the United Nations emergency force in Palestine. The five Canadian officers, all of the rank of captain, are specialists in movement control, equipment and transport. Then there was a request for signals and logistic support for the United Nations Congo force. On receiving that request, Canadian and United Nations authorities consulted as to the precise needs to be met in the Congo.
On July 28 Canada authorized provision for the United Nations force in the Congo of up to 500 Canadian armed force personnel including a signals detachment numbering some 200, as well as a small Canadian headquarters detachment. Arrangements for sending the selected personnel to the Congo are going forward, and parliament is now being asked to approve the action in this regard.
In response to an appeal for medical personnel to serve in the hospitals of the Congo, the Canadian Red Cross society recruited from Canada two teams of trained medical personnel each composed of one surgeon, one physician trained in tropical medicine and three nurses. All these are French speaking. Both teams left on July 28 and are expected to arrive in Leopoldville today. Further, in response to a request from the secretary general, the Canadian government has placed at the disposal of the United Nations the four North Star aircraft which airlifted supplies to the Congo, for the purpose of transporting supplies and equipment for the United Nations force in the Congo on the shuttle service between Pisa and Leopoldville.
In addition we are acquiring at once two Caribou aircraft from the de Havilland corporation for airlifting supplies to Canadian forces. A third will be made available in September and a fourth in October. The feature of these aircraft is the fact that they can take off from short runways. Even though only two such aircraft are available at the moment, this action will ensure that the Canadian force there will receive proper commissariat assistance.
Furthermore, we are in a position to supply six or seven R.C.A.F. officers to organize the United Nations air transport force. That force is made up of airmen from Yugoslavia, Sweden, Norway, Brazil and the Argentine. In addition to those named, India will provide certain pilots and air force personnel. This country's contribution will total 75 pilots. In order to organize this extraordinarily complex international force into a unified whole the necessary R.C.A.F. officers to whom I have just alluded will be supplied.

United Nations Forces in Congo
That, in general, represents Canada's contribution to the force. What is taking place is, I think, one of the greatest steps forward toward the ultimate establishment of an international force. Indeed, there has never been in all history anything like the force that is now being mobilized from among the various nations that I have referred to, or in all of mankind's march to the achievement of peace in the world. All through modern history hope has been expressed. In the middle ages the international lawyers claimed that the only way in which peace could be achieved would be through a force readily available to meet whatever situations might arise before they expanded to such an extent as to assure the outbreak of war.
The reason the armed forces on foot were mobilized from among the nations I have mentioned was to assure the peoples of Africa, and I think Asia too, that the nations comprising the white race were not, as it were, organized into a group or international organization against the coloured race.
I trust that the house will give unanimous acceptance to the course we have followed, for it represents a major step forward to that day when, wherever difficulties may arise anywhere in the world, as I stated in March, 1945, the nations comprising the United Nations will all make available to an international force whatever is requisite to assure peace.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PARTICIPATION OF CANADIAN FORCES IN CURRENT OPERATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, hon. members will have listened with great interest to what the Prime Minister has said, both in regard to the resolution before the house and in regard to the background for the action we are being asked to support in this resolution, including something of the history of an international peace force. We on this side of the house would like to comment on both aspects of the Prime Minister's statement.
The resolution states:
That it is expedient that the Houses of Parliament do approve the participation of Canadian forces in the United Nations operations in the Congo-
In this resolution as I read it, Mr. Speaker, there is no limitation on the nature or extent of that participation, but there is the limitation that the participation is designed to cover Canadian forces in the United Nations operations in the Congo, and cover no other form of assistance that might be required. Notwithstanding that there is, perhaps understandably, no limitation on our participation within this particular category, we on this side are happy to be able to support a resolution of this kind and, indeed the action that has been taken by the government outside the terms of this resolution.


We would say that the course adopted by the government in bringing this matter to the attention of the house in this way is the proper constitutional course to take. Also, in the matter of action that is taken under this resolution in the supply of forces, I take it that the government will table, as would be required under the Canadian Forces Act, any order in council which has been passed putting members of our armed forces on active service for this purpose. I think the act itself-I believe it was passed in 1950-requires that this should be done within 10 days of the action having been taken.
This is a new assignment for the United Nations and for Canada in its participation as a member of United Nations, Mr. Speaker. It is a new assignment as indefinite as it is likely to be far reaching and important, not only in respect of the immediate emergency which has occurred but in respect of the development of the idea of United Nations help of this, kind in the future.
We are bound to ask ourselves the question as Canadians, as a member of the United Nations, what are we taking on? Indeed, what is the United Nations taking on? A few weeks' or a few years' assignment? A temporary job in helping to restore order as part of an international police and peace force or a long job, again as a member of the United Nations, to help to administer and assist economically a state of some 15 million people which has achieved its independence in circumstances which are not easy for the people of that state? Indeed, Mr. Speaker, this latter assignment, which is related to though not specifically part of this resolution, may be an even more important and certainly far more expensive one than that which we are being asked to take in the purely police and military side of the undertaking.
The Prime Minister has pointed out that the authority behind the recommendations of the Secretary General of the United Nations, who incidentally has accepted this new assignment in his usual swift, efficient and devoted way, lies in two resolutions of the security council of which all members of the security council, I believe, approved. In any event, no member voted against the resolutions, including the Soviet union which, if it had wished to do so at that time, could have vetoed either or both of these resolutions.
These resolutions provide for the members of the United Nations on invitation from the secretary general-I am paraphrasing one of them now-to contribute forces, peace-preserving forces, for a United Nations contingent to go to the Congo. From what the

Prime Minister read from the second resolution, I think it may be interpreted as providing for other forms of assistance, because it does refer to the technical agencies of the United Nations which the secretary general might call on to help him in this field.
Acting on this authority the United Nations, through the secretary general-my information is only from public sources but I assume it is accurate-and the Congo state have now signed an agreement, of the details of which I have no knowledge, with the U.N., that the United Nations forces will remain in the Congo until the mission of peace has been fully accomplished. That mission of peace may require more than the provision of police forces; it may require the provision of economic and other kinds of help.
I am not quarrelling for one minute with the advisability, the wisdom, of the secretary general entering into this kind of agreement on behalf of the United Nations. It was well that he should have done so, but it does underline the possibly far-reaching nature of the commitments which we are undertaking as a member of the United Nations, and which we should be glad to undertake. I read this morning that the statement covering this agreement had been circulated to the members of the security council by the secretary general himself, and it would be very interesting to know whether this reported agreement has been circulated to Canada which is proposing, and rightly so, to take such a constructive and active part in this operation.
The situation, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, is not an easy one, and in many respects it is a dangerous one. There is the obvious impatience of some elements of the government of the Congo, including, if we can give credence to press reports, the deputy premier, to get the last relic of Belgian authority out of the Congo in the least possible time, to use the United Nations force primarily and swiftly for that purpose and presumably, once that has been done, to get the United Nations out also except in terms of economic and financial help. If this course were followed then, presumably, with the United Nations forces out of the Congo, the assistance given would be under the administration of the Congo authorities.
There is another kind of impatience with respect to the Congo, and that is the impatience of others at the lack of order, the lack of discipline in this new and free state, and some impatience at the administrative weakness of the present government, a weakness which is understandable in the light of the immediate background and the less immediate background of their ascension to power in their 79951-0-463|
United Nations Forces in Congo own country. So we read even in this morning's paper of rising tensions, of charges that the United Nations forces-I thought the Prime Minister quite rightly referred to one of these this morning-are in danger of assisting in what has been called colonialist intrigues; indeed, are in danger of being accused of complicity in those intrigues.
It is discouraging to hear these reports out of the Congo at a time when the United Nations is moving with speed and efficiency to assist. We also read and have heard reports over the week end of the development of separatism in this country, which has a heritage of tribal separatism, a separatism based on the historical forces of tribalism which, if they prevail, might lead to an even worse disaster than has been the case up to the present.
Then we have the problem of Katanga, the richest and most highly developed part of the Congo, without which it is difficult to see, on the basis of the information I have, how the rest of the Congo could ever become a viable economy without great support from the outside world. So this situation is a terrific challenge to the Congo and its people and to the United Nations and its members. I was reading this morning in the Globe and Mail the statement of a United Nations official just back from the Congo, who was quoted as saying:
The Congo needs artificial respiration. Ninety per cent of the technicians and administrators are gone.
The Prime Minister made some reference to that difficulty.
The government doesn't work. The railroad doesn't work. Nothing works. And on top of that tribal warfare can be expected at any moment.
I wish this were too gloomy a view of the situation. I hope that what the United Nations has asked its members to do and what they are doing will prevent the realization of this gloomier prediction. Yet it is quite clear that United Nations intervention in the situation was essential to prevent disaster. Those people who sometimes say that the United Nations does nothing except talk, pass resolutions and waste time and money in New York should ask themselves now, what would be the situation in the Congo if there had not been a United Nations to call on in this emergency?
I think all Canadians will be happy to back up anything the Canadian government may do to play our own part effectively in this essential work. That part will require administrative and technical help; and, as the Prime Minister has pointed out, perhaps Canada is in a special position to contribute this kind of help because of the bilingual nature of our population. It is unfortunate
7334	HOUSE OF
United Nations Forces in Congo that there is now, so far as I know, no permanent organization in the United Nations which could have moved into this technical and administrative field with a corps of trained international technicians and administrative experts.
I know this suggestion has been made more than once, and this situation does underline the importance of having available not only armed forces for police and peace purposes, but a corps of international civil servants trained to assist in situations of this kind. This will take a long time, but I think it is high time that the process should begin, because the situation which we find in the Congo may well be repeated in other countries which have newly achieved or are about to achieve independence.
There is the other aspect of this matter. We will be asked to contribute a contingent to the police and peace preservation corps. Once again, however, the United Nations has found itself faced with an emergency and the necessity of taking ad hoc action to meet that emergency. How much better it would have been if there had been at the disposal of the United Nations, for immediate use, trained, equipped contingents from the various members of the United Nations. Instead the secretary general, as he had to in 1956, has had to call on those whom he thought were qualified to help and from whom he thought help would be desirable in the first instance, in this case Asian and African countries, followed by help by other countries.
I think probably the secretary general would say that the principles adopted in 1956 for the establishment of the United Nations emergency force at that time have been of great assistance to him upon this occasion, even though he had to operate in a rather different way, because at that time the assembly did pass resolutions which established the principles for the organization of a force of this kind, and also laid down the principles regulating the relationship of such a force to the peoples and governments which they were seeking to assist. But this situation does underline again the necessity of pressing ahead at the United Nations for some kind of an organization which will make unnecessary in the future this kind of improvised action.
I do not mean by that-the secretary general has already expressed his own doubts about this-a permanent United Nations police force established in some particular place or places under direct United Nations control. I mean having forces available in the various member middle powers and smaller powers, kept in those countries but earmarked for United Nations use; trained


for that purpose in the administrative, technical and signals field as well as in the combat field, and ready to move at a moment's notice on the authority and approval of the government and parliament of the country concerned, if it happens to be a free democracy.
The Prime Minister talked about the desirability, which was recognized years ago by him and many others, of some form of international peace and police force behind the United Nations Charter. Indeed, the idea of an international force behind international law goes back to the very dawn of history. It has been an ideal which has inspired many men all through history, from the days of the Greek leagues to the holy Roman empire, through the middle ages with the grand design of Henri Quatre, on to the holy alliance of the nineteenth century, a kind of autocratic expression of the whole idea, until we reach the league of nations.
There was a clause in the league of nations covenant which did provide for the implementation of such force behind international law, in the development of which I must confess Canada did not play, in those days-and I am now talking about the 1920's -too creditable a part. We were more concerned at that time with keeping out of trouble than trying to prevent trouble, for reasons which seemed very sensible at that time. But looking back now at the trouble we have got into since 1914, it does not seem to be so wise.
When the United Nations charter was drafted at San Francisco, every speech made there, and I sat through a great many of them, was about the necessity of getting behind the charter and building on the mistakes of the old league of nations and its covenant; making sure, once again, that if we were in trouble we would have this kind of force. We made our own share of declarations at that time, for that purpose.
As a result of those speeches and those ideas, there were included in the charter provisions which seemed to be a recognition of the mistakes that were made in the league covenant. Provision was made in the charter for an international force which would have been strong enough not only to put an end to brush fires and to police situations with which we are confronted today, but an international force which would have been strong enough to prevent wars, because it would have included contingents from the great powers. There would have been an international force on a grand scale.
But the cold war began, and an international force of that type became merely a provision in a document about which very

little was done, if anything, to implement, except to set up in New York a military commission of the permanent members of the council, which is still in existence and which I gather meets formally every month or two.
The cold war made that kind of international force impossible. During these years, after 1945 and in the 1950's, a great deal of attention was given at United Nations to finding some other kind of force which would take the place of the one that was so abortive in the charter, because it included only the permanent members of the council who could call on others for help if necessary. I remember that at the United Nations the Canadian delegation took a very active part in the resolutions that led to the establishment of a peace observation group, and I remember the Canadian delegate, at the very earliest assembly, making a plea for the building up of this kind of international peace and police force.
The Prime Minister has referred to the difficulties in the Middle East before they broke into war in 1956, and he mentioned the desirability in the spring of 1956 of establishing an international peace force to assist in the maintaining of peace in that very dangerous area. I recall very well the discussion on this idea that took place in the committee of external affairs, when it was pointed out that the Canadian and other members of the United Nations had already taken up this question of a peace and police force for the Middle East, and that it had been rejected at that time both by the Arab governments and the government of Israel, as well as by officers of the United Nations, as premature and not practicable.
So there was the situation when the crisis and the necessities of 1956, in the autumn, made necessary that kind of swift action which should have been provided for months and years before. If at that time there had not been this crisis, it is very doubtful whether the United Nations emergency force would have been set up. Also if at that time delegations at the United Nations assembly had voted against the inclusion of this item on the agenda, on the motion before the United Nations assembly, there could not have been any international force. Furthermore if then there had not been approval by the United Nations assembly of the action taken, for reasons which seemed perfectly good to them-reasons advanced by the governments of the United Kingdom and France-for intervening, there would not have been any United Nations emergency force and we would not have had anything on
United Nations Forces in Congo which to build in 1960. It was the establishment of the United Nations emergency force which has at least given us a foundation on which we could build in 1960.

speechtext:
The Prime Minister says, what about the Korean situation. That was another kind of intervention. That was United Nations intervention but not the kind of intervention through an international police and peace force which I am talking about, because it was an intervention made possible by a decision of the security council, such as was visualized in San Francisco in 1945, but which was made possible only because the Russians did not turn up at the security council meeting. If they had the opportunity over again they would veto any action of that kind. It was also a decision to put the United Nations force under the administrative control and military direction of a single member of the United Nations, the United States of America. It was also action taken in Korea after there had been a declaration, accepted by the United Nations, of aggression in Korea. So it was not quite the same, either in origin or in the action taken, as the decision in 1956, which did set up a United Nations emergency force under United Nations control consisting of contingents from the middle powers, which is the way I suspect it will have to be dene in the future in this kind of situation.
Since 1956 there has been very little progress indeed in building on this foundation for the establishment of a permanent United Nations emergency force, for reasons which I do not need to go into now. But I think the situation in these early days underlines again the desirability of doing this on a permanent basis, and it emphasizes the misfortune of the United Nations in not being able to make any progress in the last two or three assemblies.
The Prime Minister mentioned the attitude of the Soviet union toward what has been proposed by the United Nations to assist in this Congo situation. Experience in the last 15 years has shown beyond any possibility of doubt that communist governments will not only refuse any constructive support for an initiative of this kind through the United Nations, but that they will do their best to confuse and frustrate the purposes of the United Nations and misrepresent those purposes in the eyes of the public of the country where the United Nations is intervening, in this case the Congo. Anarchy is their opportunity and chaos is their ally. Perhaps that helps to explain the sinister-I do not
7336	HOUSE OF
United Nations Forces in Congo think that is too strong a word-statements which have come out of Moscow in the last few days.
The Soviet union began to show its hand in this matter after it had given us at least some reason by accepting the original security council resolution to believe that it might take a different and more constructive stand. It has shown its hand, as the Prime Minister mentioned, by talking about aggression on the part of the NATO forces in the Congo, a statement which of course is a cynical falsehood. The United Nations purposes and the purposes of those members of the United Nations which are participating in this operation are above reproach, and I am sure all of us hope that the action of the United Nations will be as effective as its purposes are good.
We know that Canada can play an important part in this action. We learned the other day that the nature of our contribution at the present time-I am talking now about the military side of it-is to be the provision of administrative, technical and headquarters personnel. That is what was required of Canada in 1956, and there were some members of this house who made not very flattering observations at that time, about that kind of participation. But this would appear to be the way in which Canada can serve best in this kind of United Nations operation, at least at the present time. Perhaps our experience in the United Nations emergency force, as indicated to the secretary general and those advising him on those matters, shows how Canada can best serve in this situation by providing personnel on the administrative side, the signals side, the technical side, the liaison side and the headquarters side. If it had not been for that kind of work by the Canadian forces in the Palestine United Nations emergency force it would have been infinitely more difficult for that force to be as successful as it was. The Canadian forces in UNEF, as I am sure the Canadian forces will be in the Congo UNEF, were the backbone of the force owing to the essential nature and efficiency of their contribution to its operation.

I listened with great interest to the explanation of the Prime Minister with respect to the resolution which he presented to the house; that it was based on previous resolutions adopted by the United Nations security council and on procedure and practice established by the previous government. I can not help thinking-I do not know whether it is because I am growing somewhat in years-of days gone by when I hear problems of the present being discussed. I remember that someone said, and if I am correct it was a French writer, that to understand the world is wiser than to condemn it; to study the world is better than to shun it; to use the world is nobler than to abuse it; to make the world lovelier, better and happier is the noblest work of man or woman.
I think this resolution introduced by the Prime Minister this morning provides Canada with an opportunity to contribute her share within the framework of the United Nations effort toward making this portion of the world, a somewhat unhappy portion of the world at the present time, a lovelier and happier place in days to come. For that reason we in this group give our wholehearted support to this resolution.
However, the first essential is peace. We cannot carry on administrative practices or social undertakings without law and order.

So the first thing we have to establish is peace, and in my opinion peace is the golden wisp that binds the sheaf of opportunity for the people of the Congo, and we are doing what we can by adopting this resolution resolution unanimously to build that wisp. In my opinion, by this action the parliament of Canada is making quick use of the opportunity available to it in this extraordinary situation in the Congo and of the machinery at hand to demonstrate our readiness to accept our responsibility as a member of the United Nations.
The members of this group are of the opinion that the Belgian government is to a great extent responsible for the present unfortunate situation. I remember as a boy when the conscience of Europe was shocked by what was known as the Belgian atrocities, but that situation was remedied and the people of the Congo have received many economic advantages as a result of the development there. I say at this time on behalf of this group that we consider the government of Belgium to be responsible to a great extent for the present state of affairs, because there was no preparation for independence, no training of people to take over administrative tasks, no training of doctors and all those other persons whose work is required to carry on the activities of a modern state. Possibly there is some truth in the reports over the C.B.C., in our press and in United States and European papers that in some quarters it was hoped that the Congolese administration would collapse and that a Belgian administration would be required to return, together with its civil service and also, of course, its business interest. There may be truth, also, in the other reports that the mutiny at Leopoldville ruined this opportunity. But certainly from a number of reports it is obvious that there was an almost complete lack of preparation for independence.
When I consider this situation I cannot but remember the remarks made before a group of the commonwealth parliamentary association by the premier of Northern Nigeria last winter, when he spoke of that country's coming independence on October 1 of this year. He spoke of his country's long-awaited independence and said they recognized, many of them in Northern Nigeria, that they were not yet fully prepared for independence; that until a civil service staff had been trained and they had men to carry on medical services, this would not be the case. During that short talk to this group in the parliamentary association he paid tribute to the preparation for independence which had been made by the United Kingdom government.

In this respect Canada is in a particularly fortunate position, the Congolese being mainly French speaking people. It goes on to say that this presents great difficulties, as follows:
No less formidable are the civil problems facing the United Nations in the Congo. Practically all the Belgian doctors and nurses have fled the Congo; there is no one to take their place. Technicians, managers and civil servants are needed to take the place of the retreating Belgians. The vacancies cannot be filled with Congolese; in the whole vast country, with its 14 million people, there are only 16 university or college graduates.
This group believes that the United Nations should work for the reunification of the Congo so it can progress to better advantage because there will be a balance as between

That is a fair question. Circumstances are so fluid that it is difficult to give a definitive answer. I am content to leave the decision to the secretary general, the commanders and the senior officers of the United Nations.
As a result of lack of training in years past of civil service personnel and all the rest of it, the first thing to be done after peace is established will be the training of administrative personnel. That is the first thing to be done before there can be any development in the country. The second will be the provisioning and training of technical personnel. Then one of the immediate problems will be that of health of the people in this region. As a matter of fact, my recent reading has indicated to me that the question of health is a most serious one in the northern and central portions of Africa. Why? Because so little has been done for those people, although there has been great wealth extracted from the region for many years. I was reading yesterday that the life expectancy in northern and central Africa is just under 30 years at the present time.
Attention should be focused on our out of balance approach to this situation not only in the Congo but in other African states and backward nations. To illustrate, last year the United States spent in the neighbourhood of $40 billion on armaments and contributed $3,500,000 to the World Health Organization. I am not going to lay blame on any one country or the other at this time but this situation must be recognized. We are all concerned in this, and as members of the United Nations we must all share some responsibility. All I am mentioning the figures for is to indicate what one nation can spend on armaments and what it is spending in the development of the World Health Organization, which is the organization that the United Nations will use in the Congo and does use to promote health in other regions of the world.
The other factor that has been mentioned is the cost to the United Nations of U.N. action in the Congo. This is a very important undertaking. In the opinion of the members of this group it is one of the greatest tasks 79951-0-464
United Nations Forces in Congo the United Nations has handled since its formation. It may be of some duration. The United Nations may be required to stay in the Congo for some years, to the advantage of the people of the country and for the preservation of world peace. Anyone who is in the know at all at the present time knows that this is a very serious situation in so far as the western world is concerned. That is why we have to pull our weight, and no nation should shirk its responsibility.
The matter of cost has been raised, and cost must receive consideration. There will be cost to Canada in respect of our forces and in respect of other contributions, and it looks as though the cost will be considerable. We in this group suggest this. Over the years thousands of millions of dollars have been taken out of the copper mines and other mines of Katanga. Today we read-and the Prime Minister mentioned it this morning-that food is one of the immediate problems in the Congo region; that there is a shortage of food in a few days. We are of the opinion, although we are not suggesting permanent confiscation of private property, that the United Nations should take over the rich mining business that now exists and administer it during the tenure of its mandate, and then leave it to the people of the region and the established government at the conclusion of the mandate to decide what should be done with those properties. In the meantime use the profits of these properties to provide the health, technical and other services required by the people of the Congo. Surely we owe that to the people of the Congo who have suffered from this exploitation, possibly one of the worst examples of exploitation in modern colonial history. I think we, the white people, owe that to the black people of the Congo, to indicate our concern for and interest in their future, and our anxiety to make amends for past injustice.
However, regardless of our efforts to establish law and order, peace will prevail in the Congo only as a result of our continuing and united effort to make life worth living for the people of the Congo. That is the approach we have to take. The policy we have to assume in the United Nations is food instead of guns and health instead of disease. Those should be the slogans of the United Nations forces.
As I mentioned before, one of the first problems in these early days is the shortage of food. Let Canadians show their pride in the Canadian contingent to the Congo by acceptance of our full responsibility to the United Nations and to the people of this stricken area. We must do everything possible in my opinion, to inform the people of

United Nations Forces in Congo Canada of our contingent's activities while in the Congo. Today we meet a growing cynicism, a growing lack of faith on the part of our young people particularly. When this force goes to the Congo, I make the suggestion to the Prime Minister, let us make certain that its activities are made known to the Canadian people; let us see that interest is aroused in the activities of this force, this defence of peace. Let us be sure that its activities are made known to our high school children and to our public school children of an age sufficient to understand. Let us speak with some pride of our participation in this organization; let us have a continuing interest as the result of information by the government of Canada given through the press and other agencies. We must arouse public interest and pride in our participation in this very important work which I am quite sure many people do not fully appreciate at the present time.
This latest task, Mr. Speaker, of our nation and of the United Nations is a key task; it is possibly one of the most important tasks ever undertaken by that body or by its agencies. Canada's record in the Middle East, in the United Nations emergency force on the Arab-Israeli frontier, and on other United Nations teams in other parts of the world is unblemished and is respected everywhere.
In conclusion on behalf of this group I extend best wishes for a successful mission to all the officers and personnel of the Canadian Congo contingent.

Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the house, introduced by the Prime Minister, reads in part as follows:
That it is expedient that the houses of parliament do approve the participation of Canadian forces in the United Nations operations in the Congo, and that this house do approve the same.
I am assuming for the purposes of the remarks I wish to make that we are talking about the present United Nations operations and the present decision of the government of Canada, in answer to the request of the secretary general, to dispatch certain personnel of the Canadian armed forces, notably, those who have special experience in the matter of communications, that is, the group known as signallers. Anything I say is predicated on that understanding of the character of the resolution.
I well remember the statement made by the Prime Minister in 1957 at the general assembly of the United Nations when he said that Canadian foreign policy was predicated, among other things, upon the commitment, which Canada undertook as a signatory to the charter of the United Nations. That being the case, the remarks made by the Prime Minister on Saturday last, were warmly approved, and deservingly so, because the situation in the Congo now is one that calls for intervention not by any individual state but by the collectivity of states represented by the United Nations itself. Any intervention in that situation on the part of any great power would have been, as the President of the United States himself noted, a dangerous intervention. It may be that the United States, apart altogether from its appreciation of the dangers in the Congo at the present time, was not unmindful of the dangers that could have flowed from their action in 1957 when, apart from any action taken by the United Nations, the United States dispatched some 12,000 marines to Lebanon although I admit in answer to the request of the president of that country.
I believe the government has taken a sound course in proposing, as all speakers thus far have supported, that this is an action in which only the United Nations can take part. Only through collective intervention would it be possible to answer the charge, irresponsibly made, that this is an effort to bolster up the colonial power. This action on the part of the United Nations clearly is no such thing.
In the first part of his statement this morning, the Prime Minister referred to the

two basic resolutions of the security council, that of the 14th July and the other of the 22nd. The first resolution calls on the government of Belgium to withdraw its troops from the territory of the Republic of the Congo. That process is now under way, and to the satisfaction, I believe, of the secretary general. In this resolution, the United Nations also instructs the secretary general to take certain steps, among them the provision by the government of the Congo of such military assistance, as may be necessary until, through the efforts of the Congolese government, with the technical assistance of the United Nations, the national security forces may be able, in the opinion of that government, to meet fully their tasks.
There are two observations I wish to make about this portion of the resolution. In the first place, this is the first time in the history of the United Nations, apart altogether from Korea-which was an action taken by the United Nations following a declaration of aggression by that body-that the United Nations is providing military assistance. No military assistance was provided in 1956 on the occasion of the Suez crisis. The resolution of the United Nations at that time clearly authorized the dispatch of what was called a para-military body, that was to exercise an effort to preserve the peace between Israel on the one hand and the United Arab Republic on the other, through the exercise of what I call the police power.
No such limitation is provided in this particular action taken by the security council. It is noteworthy that the action taken by the United Nations in Suez was an action taken pursuant not only to the resolution of the security council but also to a resolution passed by the general assembly of the United Nations. The resolution of the 14th of July last would, I think, warrant the conclusion that the Prime Minister himself drew, that any technical assistance, which might be provided by this country, would go through the United Nations. I believe this is a wise course for the government to adopt. That would not preclude, of course, any bilateral arrangement that Canada might want to make in the light of later events. But I certainly agree with the position taken by the government, that at the present time the proper way to channel whatever material aid Canada might wish to give should mainly be through the United Nations.
The second resolution of the 22nd July recognizes the Republic of the Congo, and whether that includes Katanga is certainly not clear. However, it is noteworthy that the Republic of the Congo as of that date did include, I believe, the province of the Congo 79951-0-4644
United Nations Forces in Congo known as Katanga. In any event, the wording of the resolution of the 22nd July, "recognizing that the security council recommended the admission of the Republic of the Congo to membership in the United Nations as a unit", warrants the view that the security council by implication, at any rate, did recognize that the sovereignty of the government of the Congo extended to Katanga.
It may be, however, that the secretary general, who is a very wise, cautious and prudent man, will not seek to rely upon the general character of such a resolution in his effort to see that the trouble in the Congo is not extended, and will seek to deal with Katanga in a manner that will not encourage needless friction between that part of the country and the main part under the government of the Congo itself.
The main resolution also invites the specialized agencies of the United Nations to render to the secretary general such assistance as he may require. That too would seem to confirm the view, taken by the Prime Minister, that whatever material and economic aid is extended should be through the United Nations or its subsidiary bodies. However, I would simply point out that it may be that the international development association, which we approved in the house this session, will be one of the agencies by which in the ensuing period some assistance could be given by countries which wish to extend capital at satisfactory rates of interest in a manner not possible under the existing terms of the international bank's functions.
There is another basic document which I think should be referred to at this time, and that is the agreement announced in yesterday's New York Times, between the government of the Congo and the United Nations, presumably signed for the United Nations by the secretary general and by the responsible representative of the government of the Congo. It is, I think, a very basic document, because it clearly establishes that as far as the United Nations is concerned its presence in the Congo is at the invitation of the sovereign power. In clause 1 it is observed:
1. The government of the Republic of the Congo states that, in the exercise of its sovereign rights with respect to any question concerning the presence and functioning of the United Nations force in the Congo, it will be guided, in good faith, by the fact that it has requested military assistance from the United Nations and by its acceptance of the resolutions of the security council of 14 and 22 July 1960-
So the United Nations is there, not for any purpose of aggression, ridiculous as that charge may be, but under duly constituted authority pursuant to those sections in the

United Nations Forces in Congo charter of the United Nations which empower the security council to act in matters that threaten the peace, or where the peace is actually in danger.
This is, I believe, the most important single act taken by the United Nations up to now in dealing with situations that threaten the peace. That may seem to be too general a statement in the face of Korea, but I would simply point out again that Korea was a situation in which there was actually war on the part of the members of the United Nations who supported the declaration of aggression against the communists of north Korea.
This is the first major testing ground where the United Nations is prepared to dispatch armed forces of a military character. The United Nations emergency forces in the Middle East are not of that character; they are specifically referred to as a para-military body. The United Nations observation group in Lebanon was merely an observing group, and the United Nations supervisory force under General Von Horne in Jerusalem is merely a body that exercises police power in its purpose of maintaining peace between two contiguous countries.
All we can say is that there is no violation of the charter of the United Nations in so far as article 11(7) is concerned. This is not an intrusion by Canada, or by those other nine nations who are participating in the United Nations forces in the Congo. This is, by no stretch of the imagination, a violation of the domestic jurisdiction clause, because we are in there as a result of the invitation of the sovereign power. It may be that the question of Katanga will have to be dealt with again by the security council, or it could be that the issue arising out of the dispute between that province and the parent body will have to be determined by the courts. In any event, it is clear that whatever action has been taken by the United Nations thus far cannot be regarded, I believe, as an attempt to prevent one substantial body of opinion in a given national state from asserting the traditional right of self-determination recognized in the charter of the United Nations.
It is significant that in the matter of the two resolutions to which the Prime Minister made reference, and which brought comment from me, the Soviet union voted affirmatively. That represents a different position than was present, of course, in certain other situations in the past, all of which serve as precedents for the gradual build-up of experience in the United Nations toward what ultimately must become, I believe, the normal role of that body, namely to try and keep the peace

through the instrumentality of the collective will rather than through the instrumentality of any given nation.
There are now some 10,000 soldiers, wearing nine different uniforms I believe, in the Congo; and it is to the credit of the United Nations, to the credit of its officers, and notably the secretary general, that this organization has been effected in such a short time. The command has been given to General Von Horne, a distinguished Swedish soldier who has had great experience with United Nations troops, particularly in Jerusalem, operating both in the Gaza strip and in Israel.
It is significant that he is reported as having said that he has not yet been able to set up an effective system of communications between his multilingual forces scattered over an area of some 1,500 miles. So the particular request to the government of Canada at this time, in the face of this statement, seems in my judgment particularly appropriate; because that is the kind of military assistance which at this time is requested by the United Nations.
The Prime Minister, and I think quite properly, this morning spoke of this whole matter as a strong argument for giving to the United Nations the kind of sanctions which were intended when the United Nations charter was first discussed at San Francisco. The fact is that if the necessary sanctions have not been provided, the fault must largely rest with the Soviet union, who have persistently refused to give effect to article XLIII of the charter of the United Nations. But it is significant that the charter of the United Nations, through article XLIII, was never intended to eliminate the necessity of agreement between the member states and the security council in regard to the supply of armed forces from any contributing country. Articles XLIV, XLV and XLVI of the charter of the United Nations clearly, I believe, confirm what I have just said.
But the Prime Minister, of course, is not alone in recognizing the desirability of the United Nations acquiring a strong United Nations peace force, or police force, or a United Nations force, depending on whichever nomenclature one wishes to accept. The Leader of the Opposition in 1957 wrote this in the April issue of Foreign Affairs:
Are we to go on from crisis to crisis improvising in haste? Or can we now pool our experience and our resources, so that the next time we, the governments and peoples whom the United Nations represents, will be ready and prepared to act.
His views are supported by some very eminent people who have had considerable experience in the field of foreign affairs, among them the former foreign secretary in

the United Kingdom, Mr. Selwyn Lloyd, who said in an article written by Mr. Leslie Munro at page 210 in Foreign Affairs of January, 1960:
I have realized that it is a topic upon which one must carry with one a consensus of world opinion. The realities impose upon us the necessity to hasten slowly. I understand the limitations. It could not be a fighting force. It could only be put into position by a decision of the United Nations. Its deployment would depend upon the agreement of the countries concerned. I also acknowledge the practical difficulties.
Then he goes on:
I hope that during this assembly some indication will be given of the views of other governments upon what I have been saying.
Then Sir Leslie Munro goes on to say:
Mr. Lloyd seems to have adopted the proposal of Mr. Lester Pearson in the article I have mentioned, when Mr. Pearson suggested that "member governments, excluding the permanent members of the security council, should be invited to signify a willingness in principle to contribute contingents to the United Nations for purposes that are essentially non-combatant, such as, for example, the supervision of agreed cease-fires and comparable peace supervisory functions."
It may be that the kind of force Mr. Lloyd is speaking about and about which the Leader of the Opposition spoke is not precisely the kind of force that the United Nations through the security council decisions has asked Canada and other nations to provide. When I said Mr. Lloyd and the Leader of the Opposition, I meant to include also, of course, the Prime Minister, who has undoubtedly shared with these two gentlemen the view that the United Nations must build up in the form as suggested those forces which could in due course be used by the United Nations for dealing with particular situations.
The difficulty of realizing the kind of force that the Leader of the Opposition had in mind is reflected in the attitude taken in 1957 by Mr. Krishna Menon, the minister of national defence for India, and the attitude of other countries which regarded the particular effort as one that had implications with which they were not at that moment prepared to fully concur.
So I believe that this action represents the most important single act taken by the United Nations, apart from Korea, which was of a different character. In that case there was an act of war based upon a declaration of aggression, and it seems to me that the only precedent for the kind of action that is being taken today, particularly on the economic side and on the side of trying to bring stability to a government at the invitation of that government, was the kind of action taken in the early twenties by the league of nations when that body stepped
United Nations Forces in Congo in and effected a rehabilitation after the financial collapse of Austria. So we may today, perhaps to an extent greater than our anticipation, be dealing with one of the fundamental developments in international organization, and we hope in the maintenance of peace in the world.
I said at the beginning that this resolution is of a general character, and not being able to foresee the events which could arise in the Congo, in Africa, I believe it is our responsibility in this house to anticipate in the light of our constitutional responsibilities what situations could confront us and make sure that in consultation we will not in any way be dissipating our powers.
The Prime Minister was right this morning in saying that a decision of this character was one which in the first instance must be made by the executive, by the cabinet. Only the cabinet, under our form of government, can be presumed to be informed of all the facts involved, and it is right for the Prime Minister to say that the government takes this decision and then comes to parliament, in accordance with our constitutional practices, to obtain ratification or disapproval of the executive act.
That was the position which Mr. St. Laurent took in November, 1956, when the government of Canada proposed that this parliament should be called upon to support the resolution of the United Nations establishing the United Nations emergency force in the Gaza strip. The words of the prime minister of that day ought, I think, to be on record for our consideration and for notation at this time. I refer to what Mr. St. Laurent said as reported at page 19 of Hansard for November 26, 1956, at the bottom of the left hand column. He was referring to an observation made by the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, who had been dealing with the implications of the Canadian Forces Act of September 8, 1950. Mr. St. Laurent went on:
