"From what the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) has said tonight, and from what has been said previously by the Secretary of State for External Affairs and on other occasions by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), I feel they are with me in this, so I do not think I have to argue it. I did think it was possible, however, that the house might be so preoccupied with other matters this session as not to get this issue right into the open and have it made perfectly clear. I hope before we leave-it could be now, or later in this
debate, or later in the session, but certainly soon_
it will be made perfectly clear just how the matter stands as to the responsibility of the government

United Nations Forces in Congo to parliament, which is there all the time, but which is particularly clear and important in this matter of putting our forces on active service."
That statement by the then hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre contained the observations of a man who, whatever we may say about some views which he hold's and no matter what may be our criticism of those views, nevertheless must be regarded as a man who would share with us a belief in the strength of the United Nations in situations such as the one with which we are now dealing. He was concerned, in recognizing the desirability of giving the United Nations power in the matter, that there should be no delegation by parliament of functions that parliament has no right to delegate.
Mr. St. Laurent then went on:
Well, when that suggestion-X will not say that challenge-was made, I immediately rose in my place and said:
Then Mr. St. Laurent quoted what he said, and it was as follows:
I think the matter should be made perfectly clear at once, so there can be no misapprehension or uncomfortable feeling about it anywhere. When this bill is passed and becomes law it is the intention of the government to comply with the letter and spirit of section 33, in so far as its policy has been announced with respect to Korea.
Then Mr. St. Laurent continued:
Section 33 is the section that provides that if an order in council is passed, as the section authorizes in express terms, putting our forces on active service parliament, if it is not then in session, will be called within ten days to deal with the matter.
Then Mr. St. Laurent continued his quotation:
"The intention of the government is that if any other service should be required of this special force, which of course is not being created solely because of the Korean incident, if any police action, for instance, that has a warlike character should be required of it elsewhere than Korea, the government would of course have to make its decision, but it would immediately call parliament, make that decision known and leave it to parliament to approve or disapprove of it. I think that is the only way the Canadian people would feel they were getting the protection they expect from the representatives."
And then further on page 495:
"If anything else should be required at any future time in order to carry out similar commitments, the government of course would have to take the responsibility of making its decision, but would certainly have to place itself in- the hands of parliament within the ten-day period for ratification or disapproval of that decision."
The course the government has pursued in this matter is precisely that. That is why the Leader of the Opposition said this morning that the course taken by the government, in accordance with our traditional practice, was to be commended. I refer to these words because I want it clearly understood that so far

as I am concerned the resolution which is properly now before the house will always be considered in the light of what our constitutional practice is, a practice which the Prime Minister himself has recognized.
The Prime Minister this morning was anxious, I am sure, to establish what I, certainly, and I do not believe anyone else really controverts, namely that as a supporter of the United Nations-and he has shown that- he wanted also to establish the fact, as we all do, that the United Nations in its evolutionary process of becoming an important instrument for the preservation of peace in the world, must have behind it the sanctions to make its work effective, particularly in specific situations. I agree with the Prime Minister, and the Leader of the Opposition stated this this morning, that the reservations made about article X, for instance, of the covenant of the league of nations, perhaps especially in the light of events today, were not the kind of reservations which were calculated to give the league of nations the potential strength its authors intended.
The Prime Minister referred this morning to some remarks of his which will be found at page 182 of Hansard for the first session of 1945, when he said as reported at the top of the right hand column of that page:
Will Canada become a leader among any nations if the policy she adopts is not to allow any of her manpower to be sent beyond the confines of the dominion without parliamentary sanction?
In fairness to the Prime Minister I do not want those words to be interpreted as meaning that he does not approve of the kind of action which he himself has initiated in this instance. I take it he was advocating there the desirability of a United Nations force which would impose sanctions to achieve its purposes and ends.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the resolution before the house has been dealt with very fully and adequately by the hon. members who have already spoken. I do not intend to trespass on the time of the house for long, but there are two points with which I should like to deal.
The first has to do with the place of the United Nations in what has been taking place in the Republic of Congo. For me, the actions of the secretary general and of the United Nations are extremely significant. I agree with the Leader of the Opposition when he said that there has been a new and long forward step taken in these particular actions.
The appeal to the secretary general was made by the Republic of Congo on July 12, which is not quite three weeks ago. On July 14 the resolution was adopted which was read this morning by the Prime Minister, and which in substance called for military assistance and also for technical assistance. It is almost unbelievable that within such a short space of time there could be thousands of troops serving under the United Nations flag actually on the spot in the Congo.
There was some suggestion by the hon. member for Kootenay West that Canada might have sent a battalion. The situation is that the secretary general-and very wisely, I think-decided that the troops to go in the first place should be from Africa. This is one of the finest features about the whole action taken by the United Nations.
For in addition to getting troops into the Congo, the United Nations has been successful in having foodstuffs flown in, and is gradually providing administrative services for the new nation. I thought a listener might have taken the inference this morning from some of the remarks made that the United Nations has no administrative machinery available for a crisis of this kind. The fact is that there are several thousand international civil servants under the United Nations. From my experience in New York last year I know they are internationally-minded. They do not serve in New York as Canadians for example on the United Nations staff. There has been built up in that staff a United Nations loyalty. Many of these men have been
7346	HOUSE OF
United Nations Forces in Congo used in this crisis. Take, for example, Dr. Bunche. He was in Leopoldville within a matter of hours, and has been doing splendid work there ever since. There are a number of others from the United Nations permanent stall who have been participating in the actions taken to meet this problem which arose so suddenly.
At the present time the United Nations is organizing technical assistance for the Congo, and I understand has almost completed a plan under which it will be possible for member nations such as Canada to make a contribution which will have the effect of building up proper technical assistance for the Congo. At the present time the secretary general himself is in Africa. He has had conferences with members of the government in Leopoldville. Before that, on his way to Africa, he conferred with members of the Belgian government. I believe that the United Nations, by the actions it has already taken and is in the process of taking, may very well solve in 1960 the most difficult problems arising in Africa. The British and the French have been able to launch independent nations on that continent with great success, and now the actions of United Nations may largely round out the picture and make it possible for that continent to make progress in the way we would like to see it done. It just may be that this test which the United Nations has been facing so successfully will be the turning point in the whole process of establishing new independent nations in the world.
One other subject with which I should like to deal for just a few minutes is Canada's part in this whole crisis. The hon. member for Kootenay West took some comfort and relish from reading editorials from the Globe and Mail. I do not take quite so much comfort from their editorials these days. However, I noticed that the official opposition did not quote them; they know better.
I suggest to hon. members of the house and to the Canadian people that Canada is playing a greater part than any other nation in maintaining and building up the peacekeeping machinery of the United Nations. So many Canadians are so extremely modest and bashful about Canada's role in world affairs. They seem to take the attitude that everything their country does is just not as good as what every other country is doing, and that there are so many ways we could be improved. On the whole they suggest that we should be a little ashamed of ourselves, and all that sort of nonsense.
We have to have faith in Canada, and we have plenty of reason to have faith in Canada in so far as her relations with the United Nations have been concerned from the very


start of that great organization. We have roughly 900 young Canadians with the United Nations emergency force in Palestine, the second largest contingent in that force. No other nation with any large number of troops there has undertaken a second role in the Congo. The Swedish troops have been moved to the Congo from Palestine on a 30-day basis. This is not a new contingent from Sweden but is a temporary transfer of the battalion from Palestine to the Congo. Ireland has troops in the Congo but, of course, she has none in Palestine.
Canada is involved in this business more deeply than any other country in the world. This is true also of the members of our Department of National Defence and of the Department of External Affairs. We are participating in the various truce organizations and commissions in southeast Asia, Israel and in other parts of the world where Canada has or has had young men taking part in work, in effect, for the United Nations. We have more trained men in that category than any other nation. This is a role which we can fill very well and which we have filled with great success. These young men have brought great credit to our nation. I am sure that will be the case with the young men who go out to the Congo within the next few days.
Canada stands firmly behind the United Nations. I repeat, Canada is doing more today than any other nation in the world to help support the peace-keeping efforts of the United Nations. We are deeply interested in a United Nations force. Eventually I would hope that some sort of United Nations standing force can be devised. So far there have been many difficulties which have made it impossible to complete such a program. For example, take this Congo situation. If there had been a standing force of the United Nations it certainly would not have had sufficient African troops in it to enable the secretary general to send several thousand Africans, as has been done within the last two weeks.
The Leader of the Opposition suggested today that member nations should have forces in being earmarked for service under the United Nations, just as we have had one of our regular army battalions allocated for that particular work. This, of course is a good idea; but circumstances vary so much that Mr. Hammarskjold has not thus far considered it practical to have a standing force for the United Nations. Who could have foreseen that trouble of just this kind would have arisen in the Congo? I do not think anyone in this house would have been able to sit down six weeks ago, or certainly six months ago, and work out a plan for a United Nations force to meet a crisis that

was likely to arise in the Congo. 1 merely point out these tacts to show that the problem is not one of people wanting to have a United Nations force, but is one of working out the details. Mind you, I hope that eventually this will be done.
I am very grateful, Mr. Speaker, to have the unanimous support of the house for this resolution. I am confident that there will also be support from coast to coast in Canada, and I believe Canadians can look to the future of this force with considerable optimism. So far the United Nations has been immensely successful in what it has tried to do to meet the situation in the Congo, and I see no reason why that success should not be continued; provided, of course, that the Soviet and anyone else who is trying to interfere will just not meddle and will leave the United Nations to work out its own plans.
Some reference has been made to Katanga province. This is the most difficult feature of the whole situation. Law and order are prevailing in that province and apparently have been for some time. There seems to be quite a strong movement for secession from the Congo republic, and the question of selfdetermination arises, as the hon. member for Essex East rightly pointed out. This is a particularly difficult problem and the United Nations has made it clear that there will be no interference with the internal affairs of the Congo. For example, the statement of principles governing the use of the United Nations force in the Congo was made public by Mr. Hammarskjold on July 18, and we find this with regard to interference in the internal affairs of the Congo:
Likewise, it follows that the U.N. units must not become parties in internal conflicts, that they cannot be used to enforce any specific political solution of pending problems or to influence the political balance decisive to such a solution. It is only on this basis that the U.N. can expect to draw on member states for contributions in men and material.
We had a request by cable about two weeks ago for recognition of Katanga as an independent state and I believe a similar request went to quite a few other countries. I explained to the house subsequently that Canada had not replied to that request. We do not believe that we can help work out this problem by getting involved in it under present conditions. Mr. Hammarskjold, as I have stated, is now in the Congo or will be back within the next day or two, and is certainly well aware of the nature of this problem. I am hopeful that it will be possible for him to work out a reasonable solution. No one knows just what type it will be. Perhaps a confederation will be established in the Congo rather than a unitary state such as they now have; but Canada has felt that her wisest
United Nations Forces in Congo course with regard to this particular aspect of the Congo problem was to refrain from making statements at a time when conditions were as inflammable as they are at the present time.

Will the minister permit a question? Notwithstanding the fact that this Congo operation is being conducted under the authority of a resolution of the security council, does he not think it would be helpful to have an advisory committee of participating governments helping the secretary general in working out the principles and procedures required, a committee such as was so effective in connection with the United Nations emergency force some years ago, and on which Canada would be represented?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: There has been no suggestion as yet, Mr. Speaker, that a committee of that kind should be set up, but it does seem to me that it would be very much worth while, and Canada would certainly be on it if for no other reason than the fact that we shall have forces actually in the Congo.
Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must inform the house that if the Prime Minister speaks now he will close the debate.
Eight Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister): Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to go over ground already covered. Naturally I am pleased with the unanimity of support given to the motion. However, there are one or two observations I think I should make arising out of an apparent conflict in points of view regarding Katanga, as expressed by the hon. members for Kootenay West and Essex East.
The hon. member for Kootenay West, if I understood him correctly, contended that everything possible should be done on the part of the United Nations to keep Katanga in the Republic of Congo. By nodding his head he indicates that I have correctly interpreted his views. On the other hand the hon. member for Essex East, realizing as he must the difficulty inherent in a proposition such as that advanced by the hon. member for Kootenay West, took rather a diametrically opposite stand. Personally I believe that if the United Nations, either directly or indirectly, were to interfere in the manner necessary in order to attain the objective of the hon. member for Kootenay West, the consequences would be very serious. '
Indeed, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated in the course of his remarks a few moments ago, in the statement of principles enunciated by the secretary general it was made perfectly clear there should be no interference by the United

United Nations Forces in Congo Nations forces with civil government in the Congo. I might also underline that the principles governing the use of the United Nations forces, which were enunciated by the secretary general on the 18th July, are to the following effect:
The authority granted to the U.N. force cannot be exercised within the Congo either in competition with representatives of the host government or in co-operation with them in any joint operation. This applies a fortiori to representatives and military units of other governments than the host government. The U.N. operation must be separate and distinct from activities by any national authorities.
I feel I should bring that to the attention of the house for the reason that it epitomizes what I believe is a necessary declaration which is inherent in any organization such as the United Nations force. To do otherwise would place United Nations forces in a position of participating in civil disorder within a state, whether directly or indirectly, on the side of either the existing government or conceivably, should circumstances arise, on the side of the forces of a revolutionary government, and of becoming involved in the recognition of that government. It would be a dangerous course to follow. I feel that what Mr. Hammarskjold has set forth in his declaration is the only course that could possibly be accepted if we desire the United Nations forces operating under the direction of that organization to be effective and to be removed from all nationalist considerations.
Second, a question was raised as to the cost. The original estimate by Mr. Hammarskjold was $2 million. He found, however, before plans were very far under way that this amount would not represent even a small part of the actual cost, and the estimate now is that the cost to the United Nations will be $15 million for a period of three months.
The Leader of the Opposition said something this morning about the length of time the United Nations force might be expected to be in the Congo. There have been all kinds and types of estimates up to five years. When one looks at what has taken place in the Middle East, where the issues subsequent to December, 1956 have been less exacerbated than they are in the Congo and yet such a long period of time has elapsed since that force was set up, one can only conclude that if order is to be restored in the Congo, if anarchy is to be displaced, if peace is to be maintained, the period during which the force will be in operation there may be far beyond anything today anticipated.
I should like to make one further reference, and it is not by way of criticism. I deplore anything in the nature of an attack on any country that is friendly to us.

I am not here to weigh the difficulties of the past. I recollect the events to which the hon. member for Kootenay West made reference, but from the information that is available I feel there is every indication that the Belgian government through the years has made a worthy contribution in elevating standards in the Congo, and has made available means of transportation far and beyond those existing in many other countries of like physical circumstances. Just a few days ago I had a very similar reaction to attacks made on the President of the United States in his personal capacity. While all of us in the course of debate sometimes go beyond the limitation that each of us should impose upon himself, it is my opinion that as a general rule the best course for nations and for national assemblies to follow is not to place our allies and friends under criticism which cannot have any result that will be beneficial to us or to the freedom for which we jointly stand.
In order to indicate to the people of Canada and to our allies everywhere that unity which has been so apparent here, that realization that each of us is indeed internationally his brother's keeper, I think it only proper that we should have the opportunity of voting on this resolution, to the end that our unity will be a matter of record.

Would the Prime Minister permit one question before the vote is called? Does the Prime Minister consider the present government of Katanga a legal government which represents the will of the people of that portion of the Congo?

Mr. Speaker, there are many elements in that question. I would not want to give an answer to it because any answer I might give would not be based on a full knowledge of the facts and, in any event, if it were it would be presumptuous to make any personal determination.

speechtext:
I find that I have for a moment misapprehended the rules of the house. There being no reply on a motion for third reading it is perhaps desirable that I should say a word or two to lay before the house the outline of what this bill will accomplish.
I would list the accomplishments of the bill as follows: first of all, it consolidates and clarifies the definitions which have previously been contained in at least two different places. It does this by bringing under the Combines Investigation Act the definitions which were formerly contained in the Criminal Code. Also, as I have said, it clarifies the definitions of monopoly and combination. This process of consolidation and clarification will, I believe, be of assistance not only to those who have to operate business but also to those who have to enforce and interpret this legislation.
Second, it consolidates all the legislation under one act. It removes from the Criminal
7350	HOUSE OF
Combines Investigation Act Code certain provisions having relation to this type of trade practice and places them all under the Combines Investigation Act. This is a step which was recommended by the MacQuarrie committee. The legislation clarifies the law with respect to combinations. It does this by making it clear that the per se rule against harmful combination is maintained. By keeping the definition under which the jurisprudence has developed we have maintained that jurisprudence itself. This part of the amendment clears the air with respect to practices which may benefit the economy. This is done in the amending section 32 contained in the bill. There has, of course, been a good deal of criticism with respect to this part of the legislation, but may I remind hon. members that there has been to my knowledge no disagreement with the fact that arrangements directed exclusively toward such matters as the pooling of resources for research and similar matters would produce real benefit to the economy in terms of placing our industry in a position more competitive with that of other countries.
Third, the change with respect to the combination provisions goes on further to protect the interest of the consumer by making it clear what are the harmful effects of combinations which cannot be allowed even though those effects might be accompanied by certain beneficial arrangements such as the one I have just mentioned. So it is a fact that this legislation clarifies the law with respect to combinations and that it would be of great assistance to the economy generally by encouraging those practices which will benefit the economy about which there formerly has been doubt as to their permissibility, while at the same time protecting the economy by making it clear that those beneficial arrangements cannot be allowed to be an umbrella for other arrangements harmful to the economy.
Fourth, the legislation provides the alternative remedy of injunction or dissolution order instead of the sole remedy by way of prosecution leading to conviction now open in dealing with restrictive trade practices. Again this is based on a recommendation of the MacQuarrie committee which made a thorough study of combines legislation and whose report contained a recommendation to the effect that the provision of such an alternative remedy would be of great benefit. The type of case in which this alternative remedy might be used is, of course, the type of case where certain mergers might be concerned or a marginal case in connection with a combination where it is not clear whether or not it comes under the per se rule. In cases such as this the MacQuarrie committee pointed out


that the advantages of such an alternative procedure as against the procedure now open to us would be considerable. The committee pointed out that the use of a restraining order has been found particularly useful in such cases in the United States.
Of course, there has been criticism in this house of the provision of this alternative procedure, largely on the ground that it leaves discretion with the minister. It is true, Mr. Speaker, that the minister in the ultimate analysis will be responsible for determining what remedy is used, but that is the kind of decision which ministers are constantly required to make in a responsible system of government. There is nothing unusual or improper in it, and I think it is necessary to dispel the illusion which has been created by opposition spokesmen and others about this matter that the minister is going to be able to make his decisions, and exercise his discretion, in secret without the knowledge of parliament. That is a complete illusion. The minister will not be able to make any such decision without reporting to parliament or being held fully accountable by parliament.
Fifth, the legislation provides an alternative forum in which issues regarding arrangements in restraint of trade can be tried and disposed of. This alternative forum is by way of a procedure to allow us to bring these cases before the Exchequer Court of Canada instead of having to bring them in the trial courts of the provinces as up to now we have had to do exclusively. We believe it will be advantageous to build up; a body of judicial experts in this field inasmuch as a great deal of what is involved in cases of this type is concerned with the economic and related effects of these arrangements on the economy generally.
May I point out, however, that with respect to the change that nobody is deprived of any right whatever to have his case tried in the trial court if he so desires. With respect to prosecutions, these can only be taken to the exchequer court by the consent of both the crown and the accused, so the accused is not deprived of his right to trial by jury, if he is an individual, or, in the case of a corporation, of the right to be tried in an ordinary trial court if they wish it. As for the crown, the crown is not compelled to take a case to the exchequer court where the proper remedy is held to be by trial and conviction. This is simply the provision of an alternative forum which should provide a body of expert judicial interpreters of the issues involved in many of these cases, and

it would also provide a more expeditious method of bringing some of these cases to finality.
The next group of improvements I should like to mention-and there are four of these-is in the field of measures to assist small business and the consumer generally. The first of these important amendments is that made in section 34, which makes clear those things which may be done by way of discontinuance of supplies to merchants who are guilty of unfair competitive practices or of practices bordering on the dishonest. A great deal has been said by way of discussion of this particular feature of the bill and many false illusions again, have been created.
In the discussion in committee of the whole house I pointed out what kind of undesirable or unfair trade practices it is that we have in mind in this section and which if indulged in by merchants, would warrant the discontinuance of supplies, and there was not one member of the committee who had any disagreement to offer or suggest that he proposition that if anyone was found indulging in that type of competitive practice it was a perfectly proper and fair thing for the supplier-those supplying him with the goods by which he was carrying out those practices-to discontinue supplying them.
This, of course, will be a very great measure of protection to the honest small businessman and merchant who at the moment finds himself powerless to protect himself against this kind of unfair competitive device, the kind represented by loss leader selling and misleading price advertising, and to whom at the moment no one is able to bring any measure of assistance. As a result of this bill we believe he will find his protection greatly increased.
The next measure by way of assistance to small business is a measure which strengthens the provisions against predatory pricing practices. Those practices are now dealt with in section 412 of the Criminal Code. We have, of course, consolidated that section into the Combines Investigation Act and have strengthened it by the inclusion of a provision which makes it clear that where practices are being followed which have the tendency of eliminating competition or a competitor then the administration, the combines branch, can take action on that basis without having to wait until somebody has actually been driven out of business as is the case at the present time.
The next item in this field is the measure dealing with the question of promotional allowances. In this respect the legislation adopts the views expressed by the Stewart royal commission on price spreads and the
Combines Investigation Act views of the restrictive trade practices commission itself. We have adopted the views of those two bodies in the reports that they have submitted as to the undesirability of promotional allowances and by our legislation, I believe we will have done one or possibly both of two things: first, to bring about the elimination of these allowances or, alternatively, if they are not eliminated then the legislation will at least restore a large element of competitive equality as between those to whom these allowances must be given.
Again, under this category of measures to assist small business we have introduced a provision which will establish a penalty against those who indulge in misleading advertising with relation especially to advertising regarding prices. Under this group of four main measures we will, I am convinced, have gone a considerable distance toward protecting the competitive position of the small merchant in our economy. This was one of the deliberate objectives with which we set out to introduce these amendments.
A further provision of the bill, and a very important one introduced more lately than some of the others, is a provision which makes it clear that industry can make cooperative arrangements for strengthening their own and Canada's position in export markets provided those arrangements do not have any damaging effeot in the domestic market. I do not think it is necessary for me to elaborate more than was done in our earlier discussions on the necessity and desirability of this provision. I am certain that enough has been said to convince the house that the position of Canadian industry in export trade is becoming increasingly hazardous and difficult as a result of the competitive practices and the strength of the competitive influences being brought to bear against them and that any measure such as this which can ensure that our industry can make its cooperative arrangements in that field without damage to the domestic economy is to the advantage of Canada as a whole. This, then, is a summary of the effects and purposes of the legislation.
I should like to deal for a brief moment with some of the criticisms. The criticisms have been made on the most extraordinary basis that I have heard in a debate in this house for a long time. They have been made on the basis that measures which clarify the law as to what Canadian business may do, measures which improve the position of Canadian business without allowing any unfair or undesirable practices which will damage the economy, are somehow or other to be rejected simply because they were in troduced by a Conservative government. The

Combines Investigation Act whole basis of the criticisms of the opposition was on a basis of suspicion, conjecture and the creation or attempted creation of prejudice against this measure because it happens to have been introduced by a government which is Conservative in character.
As I said in moving second reading of this measure, this is an extraordinarily shortsighted policy on the part of hon. gentlemen opposite because as I reminded the house then, and as I should like to remind the house again, it is not as though the country itself had no interest in the welfare of Canadian business. It is a fact that practically every segment of our economy both jointly and severally has an interest in the welfare of business itself.
Men who work have a very direct interest in the welfare of business and in seeing that business is able to provide employment. At times like this when hon. members opposite express great concern over unemployment I have been amazed to find the extent to which for political purposes they are prepared to attack a measure which is designed to improve the position of business without damaging the position of the consumer or of the economy. Again, as I have pointed out, not only do men who work have an interest in the welfare of business but also the Canadian people generally have such an interest. Certainly the economy generally depends to a large extent upon the welfare of business. Indeed, the general revenues of the treasury are dependent to a large extent upon the business which pays taxes.
If, therefore, we can do as we have done here, without holding any special brief for business as though it were an organization that was not subject to the overriding public interest; without holding any special brief in that sense, if we can do as we have done here, introduce a measure which clarifies the law, which makes it clear by way of encouragement that certain beneficial practices can be carried out without danger, thus encouraging our industry to improve its competitive position; if, as we have done, we can introduce a measure which improves and protects the position of the small merchant who is so vital a cornerstone or of a truly free and independent economy; if we can bring in a measure, as we have done, to make it possible to improve the position of our exports on the international markets, and all this while maintaining adequately and absolutely the necessary safeguards for the interests of the consumer and for the general welfare, then it surprises me indeed that the bill would be attacked in the way it has been.
These will be the results of the legislation. These results will, of course, become more
[Mr. Fulton.l

and more apparent after the legislation passes, and when as I hope advantage will be taken of those proper arrangements which can be made under the legislation, these results should become apparent. But at the same time it is also a fact that the ability of the administration to deal with improper, unfair and restrictive trade practices which are still prohibited by the legislation will be made easier. The task of the administration itself has been made more flexible through a combination of the alternative procedures that are provided and the alternative forum that is made available.
So that on all these grounds, plus one other which I should like to remind the house of, I commend the bill to the House of Commons for third reading.
That third ground or third topic which I should like to deal with is to dispel the illusion which hon. members opposite have sought to create, and believe have sought unsuccessfully but nevertheless very definitely to create, that somehow or other after the passage of this bill all these things are going to be left to be decided by what has been called the process of private law. In fact, Mr. Speaker, what the opposition invites the house to assume and what they have said there, and particularly with reference to section 34, is that on the passage of the bill all those who are charged at the present time with the administration and the enforcement of combines legislation will, if they do not take leave of their senses, certainly take leave of their sense of responsibility, will lose interest in their responsibility and will lose sight of the fact that it is their responsibility to enforce this measure.
I have pointed out already that particularly in respect of section 34 this bill does not change the law, it merely clarifies it. How then can it be suggested that the law having only been clarified to make clear what may and may not be done, the officials in charge of enforcing it will be any less able or any less interested in enforcing it than they have been up to the present time? Of course, they will be no less able and no less interested. Bear in mind that on every occasion on which one of those practices which it is now made clear may be followed is in fact carried out, then there can still be a complaint made. There may be a complaint by anyone who feels himself aggrieved and no doubt there will be complaints. The limits within which those practices may be carried out are clearly defined in the act and anyone seeking to protect himself or defend himself in the course of the investigation of a complaint will have to satisfy and the same general administrative officers under the same legislation, that in fact he had justification for

taking the action that he did, and that his action did not in fact constitute one of the practices prohibited and still prohibited by this legislation.
Therefore, for hon. members opposite to talk about introducing some sort of private administrative law is nothing more nor less than for them to charge that not only the government but the responsible officials who report to the government, and whose reports when made must be made public, will themselves abdicate their responsibilities. Well, sir, of course, I reject out of hand any such improper assertion, any such improper assumption, and I assure this house that the officers who will be responsible for the detailed administration of the act will continue to administer it objectively, vigorously and fairly as they have done in the past and that the government will expect that kind of administration and itself will give that kind of administration to this legislation.
Therefore, looking at the bill as a whole, I can say safely that it should produce benefits to the economy by the clarification and the consolidation that it represents, and produce very real benefits in terms of strengthening Canada's position in international trade as well as improving the position of our domestic economy; that the measure will be administered fairly and flexibly and is capable of more fair and flexible administration as a result of the amendments; and that finally, while not in any sense weakening the protection of the consumer against the kind of practice which the legislation from its outset has been designed to protect him against, it will in fact improve the position of the consumer because of the direct effect that these amendments will have on their tendency to eliminate unfair competitive devices so as to make it impossible, or at least more difficult than ever for the setting up of monopolies and the elimination of competitors.
Surely, Mr. Speaker, nothing can be more obvious than that if we were to allow unfair practices to continue by which, solely through the power of the purse, the small merchant can progressively be driven out of business and power concentrated in the hands of fewer and fewer people, nothing in the long run could be more adverse to the interest of the consumer. It is in recognition of that principle and of the other principles that I have outlined that these amendments were designed; and it is in furtherance of these objectives that I now move the third reading of this bill in this house.

It is to just that to which I want to direct my remarks.
We heard over 30 witnesses who came before the banking and commerce committee. I classified them according to groups. The first group consisted of the manufacturers, the producers, the distributors and that class of people in our economy who are concerned with profits, with dividends, with earnings, investments, primarily. It is not an offence to be in that category. Profits are a perfectly legitimate thing; dividends are a perfectly legitimate thing, but for purposes of my discussion I want to make that classification. That was one class of witness that came

Combines Investigation Act before us. Then, there was a second class of witness. They consisted of the consumer, the person who is concerned with shopping, with buying, the housewife, the one who is really troubled by prices when they are too high. That is the second class of witness who came before us. My classification includes a third class of witness consisting of students, scholars, professors, economists, university teachers, people who make it their business to study and understand the economy of our country and how it might be affected by precisely this kind of legislation.
So, Mr. Speaker, we have these three categories. The first one concerns itself with production, distribution and sale, and naturally prices and dividends. The second class involves the consumer, John Citizen himself, who is the one who is affected when he has to do his shopping. You have these two classes, one at each end, and in the middle you have the third class involving people who in my opinion have no personal axe to grind. This class includes professors and economists, men who are academically interested in the problem. I like to regard them as a neutral voice in this debate between the two extremes. We have the producer, the buyer and the neutral voice. In my opinion the minister and the government have not paid sufficient attention to the householder and consumer. In fact, they have practically ignored the householder and consumer and have completely ignored what the scholars, the teachers, the thinkers, the philosophers, have said.
I should like to take a few moments to review briefly the highlights of what these people have said. Let me take first of all the consumer, the housewife. The president of the Canadian association of consumers, Miss Atkinson, appeared before the committee, and as found on page 99 of the proceedings of the committee she said:
The Canadian association of consumers has on numerous occasions, beginning with our original submission in November, 1951, and continuing at intervals up to our latest submission in April, 1960, made representations to officials or ministers of the government, expressing our firm and unqualified opposition to the practice of resale price maintenance in any form or degree.

She makes these statements after a very careful study of the point of view of the Canadian who goes to a store to do the shopping. Here you have very direct opposition to this phase of the legislation. I

That is quite emphatic. She went on to say:
Turning now to the amendments to section 34, it appears, on the surface, that the ban on resale price maintenance is not being eliminated but rather certain pricing, servicing and advertising practices are being brought under a limited control. Dr. Skeoch: Weil, I have some investments, Mr. Crestohl, but I do not think this would affect my judgment of these matters because, as far as I know, some of the firms in which I have investments have resale price maintenance and some of them do not.

Second, to accept the advice of trade associations-

-on how the Combines Investigation Act should be amended is a little like asking burglars to amend the law on theft or basing liquor control legislation on the advice of alcoholics.
That is so significant, Mr. Speaker, that I would like to emphasize it. The experts who came before us and laid the groundwork for the bill which the government had presented were the industrialists, the producers, the manufacturers and the people concerned with price, and it is on their evidence, their information, their representations that the minister has made such a lengthy statement today, trying to say that it will be helpful. who came from Carleton University. On page 491 of the evidence he said:

There was also put into the record, Mr. Speaker, a letter signed by the staff of Carleton University, and I should like to read portions of this letter into Hansard. It is a letter addressed to the chairman of the standing committee on banking and commerce, and it reads:
The undersigned members of the department of economics at Carleton University wish to support the views expressed by Professor H. E. English in his brief to the standing committee on banking and commerce, July 5th, 1960.
In particular, we regard the proposed changes to the legislation on loss leader selling contained in Bill C-58 as detrimental to the public interest. This in spite of what the minister has tried to explain.
Inevitably, moreover, there are many occasions when it is advantageous for a business man to sell goods below the price he has paid for them, where, for example, he has misjudged the market, changes having occurred in either supply or demand...

One is therefore not in the least surprised to hear the minister make this vigorous defence today which he also made in committee. I say to the members of this house who do represent the public that we have here on the one hand the consumer, who is interested in getting his wares as cheaply as possible, and we have this incontestable evidence from men who have no axe to grind, who are not politicians and have not sworn allegiance to any particular party. But good or bad, it must go through. In committee we were faced constantly by a well regimented majority. What could we do? We could only call as witnesses people who were independent, who stepped into the witness box with clean hands and who came before us without any ulterior objective.
Mr. Speaker, I think they are the ones who parliament should listen to in preference to

the manufacturers and those concerned with profits. But, oh no, the minister says, "Because this is a Conservative government we are suspected of favouring big business". The minister says that with his tongue in his cheek. The fact is that that is the truth, because if it were not, why does the government not take the evidence and follow the good, sound economic advice of the only people in the country who can give it to them.
We are bringing before parliament a bill for clarification purposes. Certainly no one has asked for clarification of section 34 in the past. I have heard no complaint that section 34 was not clear, so why clarify something which no one asks for? Section 34 was being very well handled and at least had some force. I look upon this present bill as being overloaded with clarity to the extent that it is completely confusing. It confuses the country, it confuses the scholars, it confuses the teachers, it confuses the economists, it confuses everyone. The only people who are not confused are the industrialists. Why? Because very subtly and carefully this bill has opened loopholes for them and provided avenues of escape.
Mr. Speaker, that is the bill the minister has brought before the house, and when the people realize that their eyes will be opened. As the president of the consumers association said, we certainly do not want this kind of advice; it is inimical to the interests of the Canadian consumer. I say that the Canadian consumers' position was not adequately considered by the minister when it should have been. We are concerned first and foremost with the people of Canada.
Of course we are concerned with business and with maintaining our economy and industries, but we have adopted a piece of legislation which has ignored completely the interests of the consumer and the government merits all the criticism which can be thrown at it. When the minister spends most of his time defending himself when at that particular moment no defence was needed, I think he has certainly fallen into his own trap when he tried to present this measure in the form of an attack. It is the old story that attack is the best defence. Or, as Shakespeare said-I am always wary when I quote Shakespeare-Methinks the lady doth protest too much. The minister certainly protested too much and has not given sufficient attention to the consumer's side in this debate.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I find it important to move an amendment. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Hull (Mr. Caron);
That this bill be not now read a third time but be referred back to the committee of the whole to reconsider the deletion of clause 14 of this bill with instructions to have power to amend it to
Combines Investigation Act provide therein safeguards for small business and against the exploitation of the Canadian consumer.

My difficulty in this matter-and I do not want to be unduly fastidious about this amendment-is that it seems to me in order to refer a bill back to the committee to delete clause 14, and if the hon. member had stopped there I would have no doubt about it. But

the hon. member goes on to say "with instructions that they have power to amend it". He is talking about the bill, I suppose, or perhaps he is talking about clause 14. In any event the committee is given power to amend it so as to provide safeguard for small business.
I do not know of any principle in the bill which distinguishes between small business and large business as such, and if we get the committee dealing with small business as a class of business, as business affected by the subject matter of clause 14, which, I take it, deals with a person accused of not supplying certain articles to the trade, there is no principle in the bill to indicate that the offence relates to a small or a large business. I think it relates to all business.
I think the introduction of that distinction goes beyond the principle of the bill or its contents as it now stands. I am also concerned about the final expression in the amendment "against the exploitation of the Canadian consumer". It is true, I suppose, that the whole principle of the legislation is to prevent exploitation of the consumer, the public, by unfair trade practices, but because of those two instructions I do not think I can accept the amendment as it now stands.

Perhaps, Mr. Speaker, you would permit me a further argument on the point about small business because that point was not argued before. The whole purpose of clause 14 as explained to us by the minister -I am sure the minister would not disagree with me-is to protect small business and to prevent the concentration of the retail business in a few hands. It seems to me that in view of the explanation which the minister gave only so late as this afternoon in this very debate what my hon. friend for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) is seeking to do is to provide a different kind of protection from that which the government considers it is providing in the bill.

Mr. Speaker, when the minister introduced the bill there was much talk of Conservative principles. I could not help but notice today that in his remarks on third reading Conservative principles were not recognized and seemed to have disappeared in a rather 
peevish attitude toward the opposition for being so nasty as to create such illusions about the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I spoke of my hon. friends more in sorrow than in anger.

More in sorrow than in anger, the minister says. I think we are the ones who might be entitled to feel more sorrowful than angry about the bill because it is a rather miserable one. The minister has had three years to live up to his reputation of being perhaps one of the most able Conservative spokesmen and also of being an extremely effective politician, someone who starred when in opposition, and in effect he did star a bit in the opposition role with respect to this legislation because in the committee we found that the minister took over some of the crossexamination of witnesses in order to try to make a case for the bill that his own supporters did not seem able to make. I thought that was rather unusual, to say the least. Of course, he has also had to rush into other committees recently to bail out government members who did not seem to be able to present the right kind of criticism to suit the government.
Speak for yourself.

During the lengthy evidence which was heard I was very interested that so many of the people who presented points of view were against the bill. Almost every group was against one aspect or other of the bill but, as the hon. member for Cartier (Mr. Crestohl) has pointed out, the academic community as a whole was extremely critical. As a matter of fact, I think you could hardly find more than one or two points on which they thought the bill had any merit.
The hon. member for Cartier has also pointed out that this was a disinterested group, perhaps the only group that appeared before the committee which was disinterested in the bill. I should like to point out along with him that this disinterest was so marked that some of the professors who appeared before the committee admitted they had formerly been employed by the combines branch for special consultation, and despite the fact that they had received a certain amount of income, not any great amount, they were prepared to come before the committee and give their views, perhaps to the prejudice of their future use by the combines branch because of their speaking out so strongly against what the combines branch in association with the minister apparently was recommending.
The remarkable thing to me about the appearance of these academic witnesses was the reaction of the government members of

the committee. They seemed to feel that these people were mere theorists. Their view seemed to be, let us get down to something practical, and the something practical that most of the members of the committee always seemed to get down to were the suggestions of the retail merchants association of Canada. In my interpretation, that of every opposition member on the committee and I think that of every government member of the committee, the reason we have what is in effect a return to resale price maintenance is largely as a result of the representations of that particular group. To say, as Professor Rosenbluth did, that to take the advice of such a group is like calling in a burglar for advice on robbery is perhaps somewhat unfair. I think Mr. Gilbert in his own evidence managed to show that neither he nor his association had a clue on the point that seemed to move the minister most, namely that small business was in a very bad way because of the fact that resale price maintenance had been banned some eight or nine years ago.
I would have thought that the minister, if he was going to go to the length of crossexamining some of the witnesses who tended to be hostile to his legislation, might at least have gone the length of producing evidence for us in some kind of statistical survey form that small business really was in a bad way because of the ban on resale price maintenance. However, we did not get that at all. All we got from the minister was the same kind of ambiguity that Mr. Gilbert fed us. As far as that is concerned, I felt that Mr. Gilbert was prepared to insult any member of the committee who was critical of the retail merchants association. How anyone could fail to be critical of such a badly organized presentation I cannot understand.
I have no complaint about the fact that the retail merchants took their brief to a caucus committee of the government members. That is strictly Mr. Gilbert's affair. Obviously taking it there was effective because it seems to have been that visit and the influence of Mr. Gilbert that led to the clause of the bill which is perhaps the most controversial and to which we object the most.
In his remarks on third reading the minister spoke about a clarification. When he introduced the bill I believe he said that this was a revision. I believe he gave us the assurance at the second reading stage that to a degree this was only a temporary move, that there was going to be a long term and more consistent approach to the matter. I am rather bothered by the word "clarification" now because this would seem to indicate that the legislation is final rather than merely a temporary revision.
Combines Investigation Act
How the minister with all his reputed ability could spend three years on a bill and come up with the hodgepodge he did is beyond me. The hodgepodge, and I think it is fair to call it that, is exemplified by the fact that the second most important change in the whole measure was brought in late in the committee hearings. The thing that bothers me about it most, Mr. Speaker, is that this change in the export matter that the official opposition so heartily approved of was brought in long after we had had the opportunity to question some of the experts to whom the official opposition is so ready to refer.
I think it is most regrettable that we did not have the chance to hear from people such as Professor English, Professor Rosenbluth, or the great expert on this legislation, Mr. Skeoch. As far as I can find, Mr. Skeoch's only reference to it was one very small paragraph, in connection with this whole business of the export matter.
The minister, in his introduction on third reading, made a big thing of the export clause and yet here, after three years, he brings it in this late in the committee hearings. What kind of preparation is this by this able minister?
I want to reiterate, Mr. Speaker, that we do dislike the export clause, for a number of reasons; that it is almost a panic move, like the panic move to bring back resale price maintenance as a result of the representation of the retail merchants. The salmon packers and the Canadian metal mining association appeared and put in a brief-and I will say, with regard to the salmon group, that if it was convinced that we were going to agree to a change of this moment so late in the arrangements, I think we are wasting much of our time considering legislation in parliamentary committees.
It seems to me that this particular clause is quite unlikely to have any other effect than to weaken the general attitude of the business community to the legislation. The fact remains that so far as our export trade is concerned, the great bulk of it is comprised of the newsprint industry, the wood pulp industry, the pulpwood industry, some agricultural products that go across the border, and certain products of the mining industry, especially metal such as nickel or zinc. I cannot see, in the present way those products are organized or used in the export market, that we need to give any particular encouragement to a clause such as this, to the organization of the export side of an industry's product, and think that it is not going to have some relationship to the domestic side.
Although the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) was close to something when he gave an indication that

he really did not think the export clause was necessary if the general attitude toward the bill in the past obtained, it certainly assumed that the government of Canada was not going to put any of our important export industries into a particularly bad position because of the Combines Investigation Act, and that there was no other course open to the minister and the branch, in the way of executive loopholes, to see that no prosecution went ahead.
The minister has gone down the list in his introduction on third reading. Again I might note, Mr. Speaker, that we wonder whether the lukewarm way the bill was treated on second reading, and the still cooler way it was treated at this reading by the government members, is any indication. I cannot remember hearing any applause, despite some of our prompting. There was absolutely no applause from the government benches.
I do not know whether this is an indication that they feel the bill is as bad as we think it is; but we think it is so bad that I would like to move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):

Where is your applause?
Yes, where is your applause?
He got some.

There are a
few remarks I should like to make at this stage, because some of the reasoning of the government has been expressed by the minister on third reading and it is completely new reasoning in so far as relationship with the other stages of the bill is concerned. One, in particular, that I can think of is that the minister when he spoke at the beginning of this debate related this bill to the question of unemployment and said that one of the things that would be accomplished by this bill, if it is passed by the Senate and given royal assent, is that unemployment would decrease and that more opportunities for work could be provided. One could understand the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) in his generous way or even the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr) reflecting on the activities of the government and saying that they have some bearing on the unemployment situation, because the winter works program can hardly be considered as a cure-all. But I think this intimation of the Minister of

Justice (Mr. Fulton) at the final stage of this bill represents a pretty desperate grasp for measures which may lead the general public to believe that the government is at least thinking about unemployment. I suggest this bill has relatively little to do with unemployment-

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I accept the hon. member's suggestion that this bill has nothing to do with unemployment and hope he will not continue on that subject.

I hope the Minister of Justice who has heard your comment will accept this indication that the bill has nohing to do with unemployment. I maintain that the minister tacked this on as a last thought.
I turn now to a few comments which do concern this measure which is now before us, and particularly that part of it which was initiated during the committee stage. Perhaps one could refer to it as the Pickersgill-Fulton amendment dealing with the question of the export trade. Unfortunately, during the time the bill was in committee of the whole and when the motion was formerly introduced by the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond (Mr. Drysdale) on behalf of the government we only had a short period of time over the lunch hour and a couple of hours during the dinner interval to go into this question in any detail. However, we did register in the committee stage our objections to the proposed amendment concerning provisions dealing with the export trade.
I should like to point out that Canada is not the only nation which has considered and dealt with the question. Our neighbours to the south have had a statute on their books for a number of years. As a matter of fact it was just after the first war when an act was passed dealing with the question of allowing conspiracies which were designed to increase export trade. Such conspiracies were exempt from the provisions of the Sherman act and the anti-trust law provided they did not have certain deleterious effects. Under the Webb-Pomarene act export associations were required to register themselves with the federal trade commission of the United States stating what their objects were, who their officers were; what instructions they had given and so forth.
I wonder if I may call it six o'clock?
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Speaker, at six o'clock I indicated that in the United States since 79951-0-465
Combines Investigation Act 1918 there has been an act under which companies were allowed to conspire for world trade provided it did not contravene certain existing laws. According to my reading the experience gained in that country under the federal Webb-Pomarene act has been that the hopes and desires of the government of the United States in passing the legislation had not been met. They found more difficulties arose after the passage of the act than previously existed. If the amendment before us were passed and an association were formed to function in a conspiratorial fashion with respect to exports it would have to take over virtually all domestic production in order to be successful. Without such control competition in the world market from firms outside the association would make it difficult to withstand the competition. This was the experience some time ago with the anti-trust law in the United States.
By dealing with the matter in this fashion there is a basic inconsistency between the act and the amendment. Under section 32 of the Criminal Code price conspiracies are illegal and' have been prosecuted time and time again under the act. This amendment would make such conspiracies legal with respect to export trade under certain conditions. This would mean that we would have two sets of rules, one with respect to domestic activities and the other with respect to activities in export markets. It is natural to assume that companies engaging in price conspiracies will come under the more liberal of the two sets of rules because they will be engaged in activities on the export market. There will be a psychological tendency to take advantage of exports, and this will encourage illegitimate action on the domestic market.
Mr. J. N. Hyland, director of the fisheries council of Canada who appeared before the standing committee on banking and commerce on June 22 gave evidence to this effect:
My experience in the marketing of canned salmon leads to the conclusion that the domestic price of any commodity which is exported in material quantity cannot be isolated from the world price. This is true whether the commodity is fish, lumber, pulp, copper, aluminum or newsprint. In this connection it should be emphasized that the factors of world supply and demand can work to reduce domestic prices as well as increase them.
This bill does not attempt to deal with the question of participation in international cartels.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is one speech of mine that has been split into three or four different sections and it is not always possible to pick up the thread immediately. However, I do not think this is a desirable amendment. While it perhaps gives a cloak of legality in the export field, its effects will be far more detrimental to the domestic field. In any event, we he-lieve that this is no place to make such changes. This is not the act under which to deal with this question. We think that something concrete, definite and constructive should have been done about our export problems some months ago. However, if we cannot deal with the shortsightedness of the government on the question of trade in this particular proceeding we will deal with it at another time.
In addition, the proposed amendments to subsections 2 and 3 of section 32, which allow corporations to engage in certain conspiracies with regard to certain matters in the domestic field, are such as to occasion our objection also. One interesting point in this regard, as pointed out by my colleague, the hon. member for Port Arthur (Mr. Fisher), is that when the minister spoke on second reading of the bill he brought into the debate the traditional difference of opinion between the Tory party and the Liberal party. He was followed by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) who also dealt extensively with the traditional difference of opinion between the Liberals and the Tories so far as the Combines Investigation Act is concerned. In view of the fact that this matter was made such a party issue, one of the interesting things I am looking forward to seeing is what will occur when the bill reaches the other place where the Liberals have a majority. I am looking forward with a great deal of interest to see whether the other place has the same sort of courage as it had with respect to another proposal dealt with a while ago.
But in any event, Mr. Speaker, to indicate formally our objections to these two other features of the bill, one of which was dealt with earlier, and the other which came in at the committee stage, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Timiskaming (Mr. Peters):
That the bill be not now read a third time, but that it be referred back to the committee of the

whole for the purpose of reconsidering section 32 of clause 13 with a view to deleting subsections (2), (3), (4) and (5) thereof.

maintopic: COMBINES INVESTIGATION ACT-CRIMINAL CODE AMENDMENTS RESPECTING MERGERS, MONOPOLIES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this amendment is
obviously more clever than it is intelligent. It is obviously moved for the purpose, not of embarrassing the government but in a vain effort to embarrass the official opposition. I am simply repeating the words of the hon. gentleman, which were rather hard to hear, in the hope that mine will be easier to hear.
It is well known, of course, that subsections (2) and (3) of section 32 which it is proposed to put into the present act-which are in clause 13 of the bill-are objectionable, and objectionable in a quite fundamental way to the official opposition as my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson), pointed out in the debate on the second reading, and as we have pointed out throughout.
It is equally obvious, of course, to everybody who knows anything about the history of this matter, that subclauses 4 and 5 in this clause would not be in the bill at all if it had not been for the initiative taken by the Liberal party in the committee on banking and commerce.
Hon. gentlemen thought they were going to place us in the awkward position of having to vote against something we stood for, or voting for something we were fundamentally against. This does not present the slightest problem at all to us. We think this whole bill is a mistake as my hon. friend the Leader of the Opposition said on second reading. If this amendment were passed it would permit the house to reconsider in committee all the subsections except the first subsection-which is after all in the present act-of section 32.
When that stage arrives, if it does arrive [DOT]-;and of course, it is an illusory hope that it will-we would do what we did before, and that is we would do our best to take subclauses 2 and 3 out. We would, if there was no hope of killing the bill altogether, continue to take the view that subclauses 4 and 5 should be in and should be renumbered subclauses 2 and 3.
But we took the view-and I expressed this, as hon. members well know, and I do not need to repeat my words; they are on page 6975 of Hansard for July 26-that if this bill was going to be rammed through the house anyway, it might as well have something good in it. We did manage to get something reasonably acceptable put in it; but we think the bill itself is bad. We think it would be better if it did not pass at all, and therefore as a choice between the two courses offered by this latter-day Archbishop Morton, we will vote for the amendment. In that way we will be indicating-and that is 79951-0-465J
Combines Investigation Act all we will be indicating-that in a fundamental sense we are against this bill.
