subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND

speakeroldname: Hon. E. D. Fulton (Minister of Justice) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to amend the Judges Act to provide salary for an additional judge of the supreme court of judicature of Prince Edward Island.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Flynn in the chair.
Judges Act

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a very short resolution and a very simple proposition and I am sure the committee will not want me to take very much time in discussing it. There has been provision since 1925 in the judicature act of Prince Edward Island for the position of a fourth judge of their high court. As a matter of fact the first move in this regard was made in 1922 when the appointment was requested. The matter has been the subject of correspondence and discussion between the government of that province and the federal government during all that time. It has come particularly to a head since the amendment to the Supreme Court of Canada Act under which appeals as of right to the Supreme Court of Canada in civil matters were limited to matters involving the sum of $10,000 or more.
I am sure that all hon. members will appreciate that this has meant that appeals from the provincial court to the Supreme Court of Canada have been substantially limited with the result that it becomes of increasing importance to provide an effective court of appeal for the province and particularly for a province like Prince Edward Island.
At the present time with only three judges on the court there the situation is that where one judge sits, as he does, as a judge of the trial court and then when appeal is taken from him to the provincial court of appeal it comes before the remaining two judges with the result that there is frequently a split decision and therefore the litigant has in effect no final decision at all. That, of course, means that any litigant desirous of finality with respect to the issues involved in his case must appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. In the light of the facts I have outlined with regard to the limitation on appeals and with regard to the expense of appeals it means that the province finds itself in very real difficulties and in fact without a proper court of appeal for the province. Litigants are in a very unsatisfactory situation in that province.
The requests, therefore, for the appointment of a fourth judge have been pressed increasingly, certainly ever since we took office in 1957. I asked that I might receive a unanimous expression of opinion not only from the law society of the province which has itself pressed this matter but also an indication that the government of the province was in accord with this suggestion as well. That indication having been forthcoming it is my view that in the interests of the administration of justice in the province of

Judges Act
Prince Edward Island this house should accept the resolution and pass a bill based thereon authorizing the appointment and salary for the fourth judge.
I might also bring to the attention of the committee the fact that it is the intention of the government of Prince Edward Island, if this resolution and the bill based upon it pass, to provide a fourth judge for that province, to discontinue the appointment of a special judge in probate matters and, as they have already the authority to do, to transfer the jurisdiction in probate matters to the supreme court thus ensuring that that court and particularly the result of the extra appointment will not mean that there is a lack of ordinary judicial work for the judges of that court to do.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this is a very extraordinary matter to come before the committee at this stage of the session. We have already had amendments to the Judges Act, some of them very recently, and the minister has told us that this matter has been under consideration since 1922. It seems to me that in view of the very important matters that this house is to consider, this sudden and precipitate decision by the government needs a lot more explanation than has yet been given us by the minister. When judges were provided for some of the courts in the other provinces which have rather more to do than the supreme court of Prince Edward Island, surely if this problem was as urgent as the minister now suggests it was it could have been decided on at that time.
The result of this resolution is that Prince Edward Island with 100,000 people is going to have seven judges, four in the high court and three in the county courts. In the province, one of whose constituencies I represent, there are three high court judges and two county court judges.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: How many constituencies?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
The population of Newfoundland is four or five times as large as that of Prince Edward Island and there is a great deal more litigation there.
It does seem to me that the minister ought to tell us why it is that this matter could not have been dealt with when other amendments to the Judges Act were brought forward earlier in the session. Why was this sudden decision made? I suggest to the minister that what Prince Edward Island wants is a causeway and not another judge, and that the idea that another judge will be appointed is not going to persuade the people

of Prince Edward Island that what they voted for last September is what they are getting from this government now.
The minister also ought to reassure us before the committee decides that this extra money should be spent from the treasury of Canada that it is really for judicial reasons and not for political reasons that this is being done.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext: Oh, oh.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
We ought to be assured by the minister that this is not being done simply to avoid an embarrassing situation in the assembly of Prince Edward Island. I am not saying it is; I am just asking the minister to assure us that it is not.
I should like the minister also to assure us that no decision has yet been made as to who is to be appointed to this vacancy; that the decision will not be made until after parliament has acted and when the decision is made a proper consideration will be given to the relative qualifications of all the candidates and not to the convenience of certain persons in that province.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: PROVISION FOR ADDITIONAL JUDGE IN PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, some of the hon. gentleman's questions are more deserving of answers than some of the questions he usually asks because he asked me to give an assurance that no decision has as yet been made as to who will be appointed. I think the hon. gentleman must have in mind the very improper suggestion that was made by the premier of Newfoundland when I went down to visit him, that if I would assure him as to the kind of appointment we would make then he would proclaim the act creating the fourth position. That, of course, is the kind of suggestion which emanates from Newfoundland, which has been reflected and echoed by the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. I assured the premier of that province that when we make appointments we make them based upon the considerations that it is proper to take into account at the time. I can assure the hon. gentleman that notwithstanding his improper suggestion for making an appointment of a judge to the vacancy in Prince Edward Island, we shall have the considerations in mind that it is proper to bear in mind in selecting the person best qualified to fill the position, as this government has done consistently since it assumed office in 1957. I can assure the hon. member that if the premier of Newfoundland will proclaim that section of their act, then the same considerations will be borne in mind and come to bear in making the appointment of the fourth judge in that province after we have put through the amendment to the Judges Act here.

He asks why was this not done earlier; he talks about precipitous hurry. The hon. gentleman must appreciate that we have considered this matter very carefully during all those months, indeed years, since we assumed office in 1957. There were a number of considerations to be borne in mind. There was the question of jurisdiction; the question of whether we could confer supreme court jurisdiction upon the present probate judge in Prince Edward Island; whether that might be a better solution, if it was one that was open to us. This has been very carefully examined by my officers and we came to the conclusion-and I think it might have been on the face of it a rather acceptable solution to the situation-that there were constitutional problems and difficulties in the way and that was not unfortunately open to us as a solution of the problem of creating a fourth supreme court judge for Prince Edward Island.
These matters have been under consideration and discussion until quite recently, when we came to the conclusion that the only way to provide that province with an effective court of appeal was by the creation or appointment of a fourth judge, necessitating a request to parliament to authorize the payment of salary.
As I have pointed out to the committee, the decision has involved discussions between this government and the provincial government, and that government has recently indicated to us that if this course is followed it would be prepared to discontinue the appointment of a judge in that province under provincial authority with special jurisdiction in probate matters and transfer probate authority to judges of the supreme court of the province whom we will be appointing.
I think most every hon. member will appreciate the importance of providing to a province an effective court of appeal. The situation over the past number of years has been very unsatisfactory in Prince Edward Island from the point of view of disposition of appeals. We find the situation so now that there is an important election appeal the jurisdiction over which by the proper legislation is vested in the supreme court judges, where one judge heard the appeal in the initial case, another judge considered himself disqualified, and threw the appeal case to a single judge, the single remaining judge of the present supreme court. Therefore, we have an appeal from one judge to a court of one judge, and I am quite certain even my hon. friend from Bonavista-Twillingate would agree that that is not a satisfactory state of affairs. But that sort of situation has been multiplied in Prince Edward Island, not only
Judges Act
with respect to matters such as the one I have just mentioned but with respect to actions involving issues which to the people of that province are very important not only with respect to the amount of money involved but with respect to the rights and obligations of their citizens which are at issue in these matters.
It is the feeling of this government with respect to the administration of justice that it is absolutely essential the people of a province should have the feeling that their litigation is disposed of in a manner which indicates to them that they have had a fair hearing initially and that they have had a fair opportunity of appeal to a higher court before which tribunal their cases and the issues involved will be disposed of and decided by a court which can in the very proper sense of the word be called a court of appeal.
It is because we are prepared to see that the people of Prince Edward Island, just as we believe the people of every other province, should have a proper court of appeal that we recommend this resolution to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has made a very touching case. Mr. Chairman, if it will be of assistance to the committee, I would be glad to make a few remarks upon the bill as it has been reported from the special committee.
I think that hon. members reading the bill and comparing it with the bill that was given second reading recently in this chamber will note that the first change is that there has been added a preamble, which appears in the reprinted bill.
Then hon. members will note that clause 1 in the original bill, which was a short paragraph containing the title, has been moved down to the position which it now occupies of clause 4; and clauses 2, 3 and 4 have been renumbered as 1, 2 and 3.
This is in accord with a feeling, which I think was universally agreed to by the committee, that the Canadian bill of rights should be in a form which would render it capable and readily adaptable to be reprinted, reproduced and framed, mounted on walls of schools, church halls and assembly halls, and other similar places, so that it would become familiar in a readily understandable and easily recognizable form to the greatest possible number of people, and especially to younger Canadians.
In accordance with that feeling it was decided that in so far as possible those provisions, having what might be described as a purely legalistic connotation, should be shortened, if that could be done, and that the framework and construction of the bill should be so altered as to remove, or subordinate to a lesser position those portions of the bill having this characteristic.
It was in accord with that sentiment that it was decided to put the title, which is in a sense a legalistic part of a statute, in the position of clause 4.
With respect to the clause now appearing as clause 1, an amendment was made in the

introductory words by way of the deletion of the word "always" in line 19. The original bill read:
It is hereby recognized and declared that in Canada there have always existed and shall continue to exist-
And so on. It was the feeling of a number of witnesses, concurred in, I think, by the majority if not all the members of the committee, that perhaps this was an over-statement of the case. I expressed my own view that there was good justification for the word "always". But as we were trying to achieve a bill of rights that would be in so far as possible the unanimous opinion of members concerned I indicated my agreement with the deletion of the word "always". I do not think it changes the effect greatly, and therefore it was a change in which I was prepared to concur.
The next change in clause 1 is again in the introductory words. There was a considerable body of opinion expressed in the committee that the non-discriminatory features of the bill were not sufficiently emphasized, and an amendment was moved to clause 1 to insert a special provision with regard to non-discrimination. I pointed out in the committee that in our view the non-discrimination feature was really adequately protected by the provision in paragraph (b). This ensured the right of the individual to equality before the law as it was originally phrased, "without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex". In this way, having firstly defined in paragraph (a) the basic rights of the individual, then giving the individual the right of recourse to the courts and protection of the law without discrimination, in effect that would enable the individual to enjoy these rights without discrimination.
However, there was, as I say, this substantial body of opinion which felt it might be desirable to re-emphasize the intent of the parliament of Canada to ensure non-discrimination as a feature of the bill of rights. We accordingly worked out a proposal under which the non-discriminatory feature could be inserted in the introductory words, and I presented that to the committee and the committee adopted it.
So the introductory words now read:
-that in Canada there have existed and shall continue to exist without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex, the following human rights and fundamental freedoms, namely,-
Then they are enumerated. The effect of that change is to provide that the rights enumerated in all the subparagraphs are now thus qualified by the words "that those rights

shall be enjoyed without discrimination by reason of race, national origin, colour, religion or sex".
There was then a consequential amendment to subparagraph (b), which I read earlier in its original form, and which now appears in amended form in the reprinted bill.
The next major change was with respect to clause 2. If hon. members will compare the introductory words of clause 2 with the introductory words of clause 3 as it appeared in the original bill, they will see there has been a considerable shortening of the introductory words. This again was in keeping with the feeling of the committee that in so far as it was possible this part of the bill of rights embraced under the heading of Part I should be readily capable of reproduction in a form which would make it suitable for framing and hanging up on the walls of schools and similar places, and that we should as far as we could eliminate all legalistic phrases and expressions.
I think hon. members will agree with me that there is no reflection or criticism of the draftsmanship because we were drafting a statute to have legal effect. I think they will agree that the words of clause 3 in the original bill as they appeared would be, shall I say, rather difficult for school children to memorize. So we agreed that this might be solved by taking some of those words out and puttting them in an interpretation clause which appears in a later part of the bill, now appearing in clause 5, the effect of which has been to shorten and simplify the introductory words of present clause 2.
Then there were a number of minor but still important changes in the particulars of subparagraphs (a) to (f) as they appear in clause 2, the details and import of which I think will be quite apparent as they are read and compared with the original wording of that clause.
The next important amendment I think I should mention is with respect to clause 3 as it appears in the reprinted bill, clause 4 of the original bill. This is the clause which imposes on the Minister of Justice the obligation of examining every proposed regulation submitted in draft form to the clerk of the privy council and every bill introduced in or presented to the House of Commons in order to ascertain whether any of the provisions thereof are inconsistent with the purposes and provisions of that part of the bill.
It was suggested to us in committee that while this might impose an obligation on the Minister of Justice to satisfy himself with regard to the existence or the non-existence of any inconsistencies, there seemed to be no concurrent obligation imposed upon him 79951-0-466i
Human Rights
to bring his views by way of report before the House of Commons. Mr. Chairman, to my mind that was implicit in the earlier part of that provision which said that:
The Minister of Justice shall, in accordance with such regulations as may be prescribed by the governor in council-
I felt it was an inescapable and necessary implication that in the regulations that the governor in council might make as to the manner in which and the means by which the Minister of Justice would discharge this obligation, the way in which the minister would report the results of his examination to the House of Commons or to parliament would also be covered. However, hon. members felt that this specific obligation of reporting should be imposed upon the minister by specific provision in the bill, and since this seemed to me to impose no greater obligation than I thought was implicit in the clause in any event I felt there was no objection whatsoever to the insertion in the clause of a specific requirement that the minister should make the report to the House of Commons with respect to his examination at the first convenient opportunity.
Then the next change is the change in present clause 5 of the reprinted bill. As compared with clause 5 of the original print it will be observed that that clause is now divided into two subclauses. This is made necessary by the addition as subclause 2 of many of the words formerly contained in present clause 2 of the bill which, as I have explained to the committee, were taken out of the original draft and are now to be found included as subclause 2 of clause 5.

Quite so, in clause 3. Those words were found in clause 3 of the original print.
Mr. Chairman, I think those are the major changes which I wish to bring to the attention of the committee. Many other changes indeed were suggested in the committee. Some of the changes which I have reported were agreed to as the result of suggestions made by hon. members of the opposition. Many of them, however, were the result of further consideration by the government itself.
The feature to which I should draw attention in particular with respect to the changes suggested in the special committee is that those changes in almost every case constituted what I have described as an attempt to reduce the bill of rights to a bill of particulars. With respect to most of those suggestions I think two observations should be

Human Rights
made. First, in many cases they were already covered in the wording of the present bill and therefore it was unnecessary to include them as specific matters. Second, they were in almost every case taken from specific clauses of the universal declaration of human rights as adopted by the United Nations.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: The Tories have all gone home.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
In case that observation was recorded in Hansard, I can say even without pausing to look around that I am quite sure there are enough Tories here to take care of hon. members opposite.
What I was saying was that in most cases these suggestions for amendments were taken from the universal declaration of human rights. The interesting thing to note, and I am sure we will have occasion to discuss this here, is the selection made by members of the opposition who suggested these changes. One might just as well ask, "Why did you choose certain articles, for instance articles XV, XVI, XXII, XXIII, XXV, and why did you leave out other articles?" Hon. members opposite are going to say that the government majority in the committee rejected provisions of the universal declaration of human rights which have already been subscribed to by Canada.
Mr. Chairman, that is perfectly true. We rejected many of them because they would have constituted a bill of particulars instead of a general bill of rights, and because in many cases they were covered already in the bill of rights. In many other cases they were inapplicable to the kind of bill of rights which was before the committee. But if hon. members opposite persist in that criticism and say, "You rejected clauses in the universal declaration to which Canada has subscribed", I would return the answer to them by saying, "Why is it you only picked certain of these clauses from the universal declaration for inclusion; why are you picking and choosing between what is in the universal declaration and suggesting that only some of them be included in the Canadian bill of rights? If they are all desirable, as we say they are, as a statement of objectives and you think some of them should be included, what do you think about the rest?" This means, with the necessary implications, that those who have said that the others should be rejected, if they apply that criticism to us that by refusing to accept them as part of our bill of rights, we are therefore necessarily rejecting them as matters of general application or statement of general objectives to be achieved by the freedom loving nations.

So I simply conclude by saying that I think the bill as it came out of the committee is an improved bill compared with the form in which it went into the committee. In saying this I merely repeat what I have said before, that there is much advantage to be gained from the calm and deliberate study of proposals such as this by members of parliament in an atmosphere where they can bring their collective judgment to bear upon proposals which are of interest to all members of the house and to all parts of the nation, where the proceedings are not merely party documents.
I know the Prime Minister in moving this proposal

a proposal which has been dear to his heart and mind in all the years he has been in public life-was proud, as any one of us would be proud, to bring this proposal to fruition. He has, nevertheless, regarded it as a document for Canadians and a document for the representatives of Canadians in the Canadian parliament, particularly in the Canadian House of Commons of which we all share the privileges as well as the responsibilities of membership. It is in that spirit that these matters were discussed with the members of the committee. I am glad there have been changes made. I am glad that a preamble which carried the unanimous judgment of the committee has been set out, a preamble which, I believe, constitutes a splendid declaration of the views of the parliament of Canada as to the principles and bases on which it is founded and by means of which 'it will ensure its continuance as a free and Christian democracy.

speechtext: When this bill which is' now before us was given second reading we were told by a long list of Conservative members beginning with the Prime Minister himself that this bill would be a landmark in Canadian history and that it would be a monument to the Prime Minister who introduced it.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
That is what we were told. This bill which is now before us after consideration in committee is a very different bill from that which we discussed on second

reading and therefore we have some reason to be surprised that this discussion in the committee of the whole was not initiated by the Prime Minister in whose name the bill stands.
Mr. Chairman, we on this side have declared our position on second reading in regard to the principles embodied in the measure which is now before us. We voted for this bill on second reading because, naturally, we approved of the principles which the bill seeks to sustain, protect and extend-human rights and fundamental freedoms. We voted for the bill, also, because that is the way by which it could be referred to a committee where the changes, for which we hoped could be made to the measure now before us in order to make it a better bill. And changes have been made.
There are, of course, various ways by which our freedom and our rights have been and could be protected, but there are many people in Canada, no doubt, who feel now that a statute of this kind-a declaratory statute, because that is all this bill is-is important in view of the changed situation of today, important, if you like, as a rallying point for a crusade against those forces which would weaken our rights and liberties; as a bulwark against attack by those forces or, as an antidote against what is more important, perhaps, than a direct attack-erosion based on indifference to those forces.
Feeling that way, we naturally hoped on this side that if parliament was to proceed in this direction we would have the best bill possible leave this house. That is our view, stated from 1958 when the first bill was introduced. It meant, in our judgment, a bill of rights which would in its terms cover all Canadians. That would mean a national bill of rights with provincial participation so that it could cover all Canadians in all jurisdictions.
We have pressed for that course from the very beginning, from September 5, 1958, when the predecessor of this bill was first introduced into this house by the Prime Minister. Speaking at that time in September, 1958, as reported on page 4652 of Hansard, I ventured to make certain suggestions to the Prime Minister and the government. One was that there should be the widest possible circulation of the bill to organizations and to individuals who had shown an interest in this question. Second, I suggested that there should be set up at the next session to consider the measure a joint committee with broad powers. I draw attention particularly to the third suggestion which I made on that occasion, namely:
Third, and this is something even more important that might be done, we should try to secure
Human Rights
the support and co-operation of the provinces for any Canadian action in this field. Indeed, as a result of consultation with the provinces it might be possible to widen the action so as to include both the federal government and provincial governments in a joint declaration on individual rights and freedoms. Then indeed we would have a powerful symbol.
The Prime Minister intervened to ask:
What are the hon. gentleman's hopes in that direction, on the basis of his own experience?
To which I replied:
I would not like to put my hopes either very high or very low, but I have learned over the years not to give up the search for an objective because it does not seem easily obtainable.
Then, a little later, I said:
I am putting forward the possibility at least of making that approach-
That is, to the provinces
-in connection with all the interest which will now be raised in this matter through the introduction of this bill. Between now and the next session of parliament consideration will be given to it by private organizations and individuals. Perhaps it is not too much to expect that the provinces will also give consideration now to this fundamental question in the light of the move that is being proposed by the federal government.
I returned to this aspect of the question on February 10, 1959, as reported at page 857 of Hansard. I asked the Prime Minister on that day:
Can the Prime Minister inform the house whether any approach has been made by the government to the provincial governments in respect of the adequacy or otherwise of this particular bill?
The Prime Minister replied:
The answer would be a simple no, Mr. Speaker, but I do not think that would cover the situation. The hon. gentleman will remember that some years ago, while one or other of those committees was sitting, the provinces were communicated with and the attorneys general of the several provinces asked for their opinions and reactions. At that time it seemed to be generally accepted by the government of that day that a bill of rights in the form of an amendment to the constitution which would cover not only those rights that are specifically allotted to parliament but as well those which fall withm provincial jurisdiction was not acceptable to many of the provinces.
As recently as July 1 of this year, as reported at page 5648 of Hansard, only a few weeks ago, the Prime Minister said:
As far as constitutional amendment is concerned, it is impossible of attainment at this time.
The hon. member for Vancouver East interjected, "Why?"
The Prime Minister replied:
Simply because of the fact that the consent of the provinces to any interference with property and civil rights cannot be secured.
We know that as late as July of this year no effort was made by the government to approach the provinces to see if some progress

Human Rights
could not be made in converting this bill into a national bill of rights. We were told that it would be a waste of time, that there would be no possibility of success in that direction.
Surely the events of last week at the conference between the federal and provincial governments demonstrated conclusively that it would not have been a waste of time during those two years to have consulted with the provinces on this important matter. The government has now been prodded by the provinces themselves to do what this government should have been doing during the last two years and that is to discuss together the possibility of a national bill of rights made possible through constitutional amendments.
Instead of taking that course the government decided to press ahead with the passage of a federal bill or rights limited to matters under federal jurisdiction. The government having taken that position, as I said, when the bill was brought before us on second reading we supported it and we supported sending it to a committee so that it could be examined but we did object strenuously to the procedure which was followed in regard to the consideration given to this matter as a federal matter. That procedure as we see it has been entirely unsatisfactory in regard to the importance of this matter and the time that should have been allotted to its consideration by this parliament and by those outside parliament who are as interested in this matter as we are. Indeed, in our view that has been an example of how not to proceed in regard to a matter of such vital importance.
We recall, and it is already on the record in the debate on second reading, that an assurance was given by the Prime Minister last September that early this session the bill would be submitted to a joint committee of both houses. That is what we had asked for and what we continued to ask for in this session. As early as January 19, 1960, I believe only four days after parliament convened, I asked the Prime Minister if he would:
-inform the house whether it is his intention to send the bill of rights to a committee, and if so, what kind of committee?
The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, when the bill of rights is introduced there will be a discussion and an indication as to the procedure to be followed.
I then asked:
Mr. Speaker, I ask the Prime Minister if he does not think it would be fair to the opposition to let them know in advance of the introduction of the bill and the procedure which will be followed with regard to its later consideration.

The Prime Minister said:
I agree entirely.
The question was brought up again on February 10 by the hon. member for Cartier, who asked the Prime Minister:
Can the Prime Minister inform the house when he plans to introduce the bill of rights, and does he plan to set up a parliamentary committee to which he will refer the bill for study?
The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, when the house leader is here and it becomes convenient to indicate the date of introduction, the entire process to be followed will then be made clear to members of the house, well in advance of the beginning of discussion.
We waited for a while. The next question asked on this side of the house was asked by the hon. member for Skeena on March 11 when the hon. gentleman inquired:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question to the Prime Minister, and ask if he could give any indication to the house as to when we might expect the introduction of the proposed bill of rights.
There was a characteristic interjection by an unidentified hon. member who said:
As soon as you stop talking.
The Prime Minister replied:
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter I am most anxious to have proceeded with at the earliest possible date, but for some reason we are not making the progress that would permit introduction of this important measure.

Then on June 8, after a lapse of some weeks, I asked the Prime Minister if he could tell us then and we were told, as reported at page 4661 of Hansard that in a few days he hoped to be able to let the house know when the bill would be proceeded with. On June 22 the question was brought up again and the Prime Minister said he hoped to be able to tell us the next week on Wednesday or Thursday subject to considerations arising out of conversations between the party leaders.
This is the record of our attempt to find out when the bill would be introduced. Having been assured that it would be introduced as soon as possible and that there would be ample consideration in advance so hon. members of the government and the opposition could prepare for the work of the committee, on June 28 we were told that on July 1 the bill would be introduced and that the committee which would be set up could take all the time that was required to consider it no matter how long they were required to meet in session during the summer. As we know the committee was set up. It obviously worked under great pressure because of the timing of its setting up.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: The only pressure was that of the hon. member for Essex East.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
It was a committee that we were promised would have every opportunity to do its work, carefully assess the bill, summon witnesses from outside and carry on its work without unnecessary interference with hon. members' duties in the house. That committee was set up in the first week of July. The minister may say what he likes but that is the way the government carried out its promise and the commitment we had every reason to believe we had secured as to the way this matter would be dealt with in this House of Commons, this matter which was of such vital importance, so we were told, to the people of this country.
No one can say that in the way the committee worked, because of the pressure of time and because we were approaching the end of our session, there was the same opportunity for careful consideration, with witnesses to be summoned from all the provinces if they were interested, the kind of consideration that could have been given if the committee had been set up earlier in the session. That is no reflection on the work that was done in the committee because it worked under great pressure and in the face of those difficulties some very splendid work was done. As a result of that work we have a much better bill.
The minister mentioned some of the changes that were introduced in the committee. He did not mention all of them. The record of the committee hearings will show how those changes were brought about, and the constructive efforts that were made by members on this side to improve this bill, and the results of those efforts.
Tonight the minister had something to say about the improvement of the bill with regard to the inclusion of a preamble, a preamble couched in such terms that it would be suitable for display to school children, for wall display, and all that kind of thing. I think it is a good preamble. But the minister may also remember that when on second reading we on this side talked about the desirability of having a preamble, of making this bill an impressive one for the very purpose which the minister mentioned, we were laughed at and the minister asked, did we want a bill or poetry.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: That had no relation to the preamble.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
We have a preamble now, and I say it is a good one. It is one change which makes it a better bill. There are other changes which will be dealt with by my colleagues on this side, particularly by those
Human Rights
who worked on the committee. Many of the other proposals that were made on this side were rejected. We shall have an opportunity to bring them forward, if we so desire, during the committee proceedings. One thing we would like to have seen done, and had there been more time for consideration perhaps it might have been possible, I do not know, was this. The suggestion was made that it would have been a good thing if this bill could have been divided into three bills: the first a declaratory bill which would stand by itself on its own merits; the second a bill which would deal with the Interpretation Act, and the third a bill which would deal with amendments to the War Measures Act. That, however, was not possible; certainly it would not have been possible at this time.
We on this side attach very great importance to the amendment which has been made and the amendments which we have proposed to the War Measures Act and we shall return to those amendments during the discussion of the bill in committee.
I did not have the privilege of attending the hearings of the committee, but I read most of the record of those hearings and I well remember how Professor Lower emphasized that there could be no sure protection of the rights of the individual in any bill or in any legislative enactment that does not deal with war measures, which does not deal with emergencies of wartime and the necessity for protecting rights and freedom during the atmosphere of war or apprehended war. During the hearings in the committee we on this side did try to get some further amendments, or would have tried to get some further amendments, to the War Measures Act along the lines that we had proposed on second reading, but our proposals to that end were ruled out of order on what seems to me the extraordinary ground that this bill was dealing with rights; that it was a bill of rights and therefore it was out of order to move anything that concerned the War Measures Act, even though in this bill of rights there had already been made one amendment to the War Measures Act. We shall have an opportunity now, as I have said, to bring forward again some of those amendments, to discuss them and I hope to convince the committee that they will mean further improvement to this bill, if they are adopted.
As I have said, a study of the proceedings and evidence of the committee will show not only that this bill has been improved but how the improvement was brought about. Some of the confusion and uncertainty which we feel would have been created by the terms of the bill originally in regard to the legal

Human Rights
situation in Canada have, I think, been removed by the changes that have been made. There have been some additions to the bill which I think strengthen its provisions and are designed to strengthen rights and freedom. It is a better bill as the result of the work the committee has given to it. It could have been an even better bill if the committee had more time to consider this matter, and had there been more witnesses called before the committee.
I understand that-perhaps I will be corrected if I am wrong

there was not a single witness from the province of Quebec before the select committee except Professor Scott.

speechtext: What about Cohen?

speechtext: Shall I put it this way. There was not a single French speaking witness before the committee; I do not think there was one.

speechtext: Mr. Dorion was there.

speechtext: Mr. Dorion was a member of the committee, and a very valued one, as anyone will gather from reading the record. It seems to me he played a very constructive part in the work of the committee. It is a better bill, Mr. Chairman, because of what the committee has done. We are now in committee of the whole. It is our aim on this side to make it a better bill still.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, over the years the C.C.F. has been interested in parliament adopting a bill of rights. As a matter of fact, even before the Prime Minister advanced a case for a bill of rights members of this group had been promoting a Canadian bill of rights.
The bill before us this evening is entitled "Bill C-79". Of course, it has the same number and the same title as the original bill, but it is a measure that has had prolific changing and I would think on a quick glance that the bill has probably about 50 per cent of the words that were in the original bill, and about 50 per cent of them have been added since the bill went to committee.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: The hon. member had better look again.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Take a longer look.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
I have in my hand the bill containing the deletions and the bill containing the additions. I have not counted the words, but I venture to say about half of the words in the new bill were not in the first bill that came before this house and I think that is all to the good. I think the bill is a better bill because of the changes made in the committee.

One particular amendment that I think is valuable is the one having to do with clause 2 which reads:
Every law of Canada shall, unless it is expressly declared by an act of the parliament of Canada that it shall operate notwithstanding the bill of rights, be so construed and applied-
And so on. I think this is a particularly good amendment which strengthens the bill of rights.
We have advocated over the years that a Canadian bill of rights would be better embedded in the Canadian constitution. We still hold that view. We feel that the government has not taken every opportunity to accomplish this desirable end but rather there has been a determination on the part of the Prime Minister and the government to have a second-class measure when a first-class measure might have been attained. As I see it, the original bill presented to the committee was a rather naked bill. The committee has partially clothed the bill but if we are to have a fully clothed bill of rights then in my judgment it must be a bill of rights that is embedded in the constitution.
The Prime Minister has not been in a rush to put the bill through parliament since he took office. The rush has occurred toward the end of this session. A similar measure was introduced in the house in 1958 and almost two years have elapsed until our discussion now of this bill in its nearly final form. What has the government done in that two-year period to obtain an agreement with the provinces so that we might have an amendment to the constitution? As far as I know, it has done nothing. As far as I know the government has made no effort whatsoever to obtain from the provinces their consent to an amendment to the constitution.
When the bill was introduced for the first time this session I said in the debate that, although the premier of Saskatchewan had written to the Prime Minister in January, 1959 setting forth the position of that province and asking the Prime Minister to take the initiative in calling a federal-provincial conference, the Prime Minister had not so much as replied to the letter of the premier of Saskatchewan up to then or, in fact, up to the present time. It is true that an executive assistant acknowledged the letter of the premier but I think it is not an adequate reply to delegate the government's answer to an executive assistant when the premier of Saskatchewan had made a sincere proposal that certain action should be taken in order to bring about an amendment to the Canadian constitution.
Many witnesses came before the special committee and I think the deliberations of

the committee were very valuable. I believe that a suggestion was made to the committee as to how a constitutional amendment might in time be obtained even if agreement on the part of all the provinces could not be achieved at this time. Professor Frank Scott in his evidence as reported on page 24 of the proceedings of the committee, put forward the idea that there should be an amendment to the Canadian constitution which would remove from parliament the right to interfere with certain basic rights and fundamental freedoms and that along with such a constitutional amendment, which was in every way the right of the federal parliament, there should be provision made whereby a provincial government through its legislature could by legislative action forego the authority within the provincial jurisdiction to interfere with the same kind of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
The immediate result of this kind of provision would be to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms is so far as the right of parliament to interfere is concerned and to enable the provinces, if they wished, further to protect human rights within the provinces from interference by the legislatures. It was the opinion of Frank Scott, and I think it is a sound opinion, that after a few years one province after another would take this action and that within the near future we would in fact have a constitutional bill of rights that would apply, not only to the federal jurisdiction but also to the jurisdiction of all the provinces after action by the legislatures of those provinces.
This the government has not done. Instead we have before us tonight this bill of rights which in my view is not the best way to protect human rights and fundamental freedoms. The Prime Minister has not canvassed the provinces. Even when one provincial premier wrote to the Prime Minister asking for action to provide a method of obtaining a constitutional amendment there was no reply.
At the federal-provincial conference just concluded it was suggested by the premier of Quebec that there should be a conference for the purpose, not only of domiciling the Canadian constitution within Canada but also so that action could be taken to obtain a constitutional bill of rights. I think that may be the break-through in obtaining a constitutional amendment to provide for a Canadian bill of rights. In my opinion this presented a great opportunity to the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister could have informed the provinces that there would be a federal-provincial conference called at
Human Rights
the request of the provinces to hear their views on this question and to take a concrete step forward by agreement to provide a bill of rights in the constitution. Instead, orders have gone out to the Conservative party: "We are going to have this bill of rights, admittedly with amendments, but this is to be the bill of rights".
I expressed the opinion in the committee, and I hope I am wrong, that once this bill becomes law it may in fact delay the time when we can have a constitutional amendment because some of the provinces may well say: "We have a bill of rights so let us not do anything more; let us wait until it is tested in the courts; let us give it time to see whether or not it works." By giving it time, perhaps a very long time, a constitutional amendment may not be possible.
I think the government has taken a rather arrogant approach by its attitude that parliament will pass this bill of rights here and now, that although it was admitted in the committee by the Minister of Justice that a constitutional amendment is preferable they will not take steps at this time to bring about a constitutional amendment through consultation and action with the provinces. This attitude, which is one of they will do it themselves even if it is second best, is the attitude that the government has taken on this question for a period of two years now. I believe that the bill is a better bill than when it went to the committee. There is no doubt in my mind that parliament will give this measure its overwhelming approval but nevertheless this is not the best type of bill of rights that in my view might have been obtained.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: What is wrong with it?

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
The government has said: "No, we will not consult the provinces, we will not have a constitutional amendment; we will be satisfied with merely another statute on the statute books of the country". We in this group look forward to the day when there will be a constitutional amendment. The fight for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms has been a long one and will be a continuing battle.
This bill is not perfect and its imperfections are bound to be seen in the days ahead. If we had the most perfect measure within our constitution, then the great battle within Canada for equality, human rights and fundamental freedoms would still be a continuing one; would require the support of the Canadian public; would require a view of tolerance by all Canadian

Human Rights
citizens. This battle for equality, for recognition, for human rights and fundamental freedoms will be continued. Undoubtedly this measure marks for Canadians a step, even though an inadequate step, forward.
We look to the day when we shall have a constitutional amendment. We think the attitude of this government has delayed that kind of amendment; but we think if the provinces, led by Saskatchewan in 1947 by its provincial bill of rights, continue to press the federal government, if public opinion continues to impress itself upon the government, and if this government should remain in office long enough perhaps we shall see initiative from this government toward a constitutional amendment.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am glad to have the opportunity of saying a few words on this all-important question. I am glad this bill has been introduced. I am glad that we had a committee. I am glad that it has been so much discussed, because I think it is a good thing for us to turn away occasionally from finance and taxation, from combines and tariffs, and to spend some time in thinking about the basic things that enter into the society in which we live together. That is what I have been doing. I was not a member of the standing committee, but I was able to attend a good many of the sessions. I really feel it was worth while to be spending time hearing our own members and others whose opinions were worth while discussing these grave matters.
Of course, when you begin to discuss rights and freedoms you immediately run into duties and responsibilities, and when you have those four united you have a very large part of our life together. I should like at the very outset to say what the Minister of Justice has already said, that I think we owe a great deal to the Prime Minister in this matter. I shall refer to this later; but at the very outset-

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: MEASURE PROVIDING FOR RECOGNITION AND PROTECTION OF HUMAN RIGHTS AND FUNDAMENTAL FREEDOMS
speechtext:
-I want to quote what Professor Lower said. He was formerly in the west and is now at Queen's University:
I would like to pay my humble tribute to the Prime Minister of the country for having brought in this bill. He has forced discussion on an issue which I suppose in ordinary times most people do not give much attention to. I think it was commendable on his part and I am sure it will be infinitely useful in the future.
The Prime Minister, year after year after year, has brought up this matter, ever since I have been in this House of Commons and before.
I suppose it is merely stating the obvious to say that it is of special importance for us

to try to turn our minds back to the serious things in our society in this strange new world in which we are living today. If one looks back half a century he realizes that at the end of the Victorian era the world seemed a settled world in which parliamentary democracy would spread over the whole world, and progress was assured.
What has happened in these last 50 years? Everything seemed set fair in 1909 or 1910. We had no knowledge of the explosions which awaited us. Therefore, I say it is a good thing for us to recall our rights and freedoms and how they arose.
I am often astonished at the height to which our forefathers rose in establishing justice and I would like to recall this. I propose to read' to you a few words from the great Earl of Chatham, describing in eloquent terms the position of the law in England. Incidentally, I might mention the fact that Voltaire, when he visited England, pronounced the laws harsh, but noted that they were the same for all. Having found out that that was not the case in Prance, he thought it was a good thing. While speaking about the rule of law, I should like to read a few sentences from the Earl of Chatham, in his speech on the excise bill, where he puts in eloquent terms the position of the law in England:
The poorest man may In his cottage bid defiance to all the force of the crown. It may be frail; its roof may shake; the wind may blow through it; the storms may enter, the rain may enter-but the King of England cannot enter; all his forces dare not cross the threshold of the ruined tenement.
I think you will agree that that is an astonishing tribute to the rule of law, and yet it is a plain statement of fact. I want to add a word also from that great politician, and I might say he was a Conservative politician, Edmund Burke. If it sounds highfalutin', let me say it is a statement of fact. Here are his words:
God who gave our nature to be perfected by our virtue, willed also the necessary means of its perfection. He willed therefore, the state,... but the state ought not to be considered as nothing better than a partnership agreement in a trade of pepper and coffee, calico or tobacco, or some other such low concern, to be taken up for a little temporary interest, and to be dissolved by the fancy of the parties. It is to be looked on with other reverence; because it is not a partnership in things subservient only to the gross animal existence of a temporary and perishable nature. It is a partnership in all science; a partnership in all art; a partnership in every virtue, and in all perfection.
These are noble words, and we hardly feel that pedestrian people like ourselves can keep up with them. But nevertheless our rights and freedoms never would have arisen

but for the fact that generation after generation produced such men who could induce other people, for the moment at any rate, to rise to their own level.
Some of you will remember with affection and respect one of our former fellows in this House of Commons, the late John Hackett. John Hackett served a term as chairman of the Canadian Bar Association. He tried hard to make the legal profession feel that law was not merely a means of earning a livelihood, but one of the pillars of the state. John Hackett used to say the law was just Christianity put into practice. It sounds very highfalutin', as I said a moment ago; but if you take some of the circumstances of law and look at them, I think they reach the highest standard of fairness between men.
I always think of the law of trusteeship in this regard. I will give you one illustration. Trustees, as we all know, are limited to certain types of investments usually called trustee investments. If a trustee makes an unauthorized investment and by so doing makes a loss for his beneficiary, he is responsible. On the other hand, if he makes a profit, he cannot keep that; he has to hand it over.
I think that is a very high standard of conduct, and I like to think that is demanded by law. Furthermore, I think if we pause to think of rights and freedoms, duties and responsibilities, we reach human affairs at the highest level, and I think we also reach international relations. I think we reach the question when we are reflecting on that; as a nation have we any serious purpose; what are we doing?
Not long ago this question was easy; we felt we were pioneers developing a new country and we felt that was a serious purpose. The world has shrunk since then. Even 15 years ago, when Wendell Wilkie wrote his book "One World", it was very unconvincing to us. It seemed very unreal; it did not seem to come home to us very much. Now, by jet plane we live next door to each other; foreign relations become a matter of day to day consideration.
I have already quoted in this house remarks of that remarkable woman Barbara Ward, and I want to quote one paragraph again now.
As the world enters the 1960's one fact seems sure. The pace of revolutionary change in every sphere of human affairs will gather momentum.
And again:
What, in these circumstances, will be the response of the western powers? The answer depends not only upon the new political leadership available in the west; it depends profoundly upon the sort of people the free nations have become as they face the mounting crises of their age.
Human Rights
I make no apology for these quotations because I think we are either going to live up to them in some measure or we are going to suffer. Because of this I feel grateful to the Prime Minister in forcing upon us through this bill a discussion of this matter.
We all know that the Prime Minister has devoted himself to the subject. One of my earliest recollections of my first parliament in 1945 was the Prime Minister bringing up the question then, I think in connection with emergency powers. I have checked the intervening years and I have been amazed to find that in practically every year this question has been raised by the Prime Minister. When I first heard him speak on this I was one of those who was a little afraid of putting rights and freedom in writing instead of relying on custom and tradition for fear that the written word might unintentionally have a limiting effect. But I have changed my mind as I have heard this question debated and advocated through the years.
When I read the Prime Minister's speeches of July 1 and July 7, I found in it a moving culmination of many years of patient advocacy. Let me quote briefly from Hansard of July 7:
I view this bill of rights as a statement of a Canadian sense of history and of the objectives and standards that we accept in the fashioning of the society in which we believe. I know it has been said before by the cynics, who believe themselves realists, that declarations mean nothing... My answer to those who hold that view is that the same arguments could have been used against the sermon on the amount and compared with the actual practices of those of us who are Christians... I am a realist, but X do hold this to be true-that in the years ahead we shall look back upon this as a measure that showed we had faith in our institutions; that we intended to assure the individual that the rights that he has inherited will not be diminished...
Those were my aspirations as an ordinary Canadian now having the opportunity, in a country that gives opportunity, to bring before parliament that which X believe to mean much to Canada.
I would now like to go back for a moment to 1947 and indicate to you how the Prime Minister has followed up the principles he has expressed. As reported on page 3158 of Hansard for May 16, 1947, the Prime Minister said:
To be effective, a bill of rights must represent, as my right hon. friend said today, the philosophy of the human being, and of a free people. It must deny the right of any government to interfere with my right to speak within the law; my right to serve my Maker as my conscience demands; my right to be free from the threats of a police state, whether consciously or unconsciously administered; my right to live my own life within the limits of the law, without regard to race or colour or creed; my right to belong to an unpopular minority anywhere in this country; my right to have recourse to the courts to guard me against the intrusions or the invasions of the state.

Human Rights
So, Mr. Chairman, you will see how views have remained unchanged, and how this has carried on down through the years.
I propose to say very little about the legal points in this bill; I will leave that to others more qualified than myself. But I would like to refer to two witnesses who came before the committee. One of them was Professor Frank Scott, and while it is quite true that Professor Frank Scott was critical of the bill, he said one thing which interested me and which I think is worth quoting, because it seems to me to be an answer to the criticism of colonialism. He said:
We are going to have to bring to Canada the power to amend every portion of the British North America Act by some agreed procedure, a procedure which will undoubtedly involve some degree of provincial participation. However, until we do that I do not think there is anything un-Canadian or unpatriotic, or unnationalistic for us to utilize the machinery we have, and the United Kingdom parliament is still part of our constitutional machinery. We turn it on when we want to, and turn it off again. It is an odd situation only explainable in historical terms. For that reason I do not think we should hesitate to employ this procedure where it is appropriate.
I would also like to refer briefly to Professor Lower. He was very definite as to the desirability of going ahead with the bill although he had certain criticisms of it, particularly with regard to the War Measures Act. There was a conversation between him and the Minister of Justice on that point, as a result of which Professor Lower professed himself much more satisfied and less worried. I think the Prime Minister has cleared away that difficulty now by agreeing that the War Measures Act may be reviewed.
As I see it, this bill before the committee has been improved and has been studied by the special committee. It has now come back to us. The Minister of Justice appeared before the committee on several occasions and showed two things; first of all, a mastery of his subject and, second, courtesy and patience in dealing with criticisms and the amendments, accepting certain of them. In these circumstances it seems to me the situation before us now is that the bill has been studied and therefore there is no reason for delay.
These constant references to the provinces leave me somewhat unmoved, because experience has shown that it is not too easy to get eleven governments to agree. One must remember also that there are provinces which are Liberal, provinces which are Conservative, two I think are Social Credit and one is C.C.F. It is conceivable that when they all get together they may have differences between them. In any event it seems to me that this bill as it stands before us deals with matters which go to the very roots of our

life at a time when we need to consider the basis of our life very seriously.
I remember being struck very much with a speech made some years ago by a well-known journalist, a man whose attitude towards communism is the same as that of any hon. member in this committee. He said that we faced one thing. He said that the communists have a something; we may find it abominable but nevertheless they have a something to which they are devoted, and he said that we will never defeat a something with a nothing. For that reason, Mr. Chairman, I am glad we have had the chance to examine some of our basic principles. I hope we will find time to think about this, and if we do not think about it in this chamber, who is going to think about it? I read an article the other day by an American who had just come back from Moscow. He had flown from Moscow to Miami and expressed great shock. In Moscow he found what he thought was a much better way of life, superficially at any rate, than that in Miami. He found people worked hard in Moscow. I understand, for example, that the sale of books in Moscow is far, far ahead of this country. This American found the Russians hard working and devoted to serious things, and that when he got to Miami he found that the most obvious thing was the pursuit of pleasure-two, three or four cars in the garage, and so on. He did not think that was showing any sign of serious purpose in life, and he thought a serious purpose was necessary. Therefore if consideration of this bill moved us in the slightest toward that end, I think it has been well worth while. (Translation):

Mr. Chairman, during the previous discussion on second reading of the bill, I made a few remarks and, on that occasion criticized the legislation then submitted to us, which of course did not contain the amendments it now contains. I now want to recall a few of my criticisms.
At that time, I first of all said that the bill was too limited in scope; second, that it gave rise to uncertainties with regard to constitutional problems; third, that I was among those who thought it preferable to try, by all means, to have a national bill of rights by amending the constitution in order to obtain provincial co-operation in working out such an amendment; fourth, I mentioned, like other members of our group, that the bill of rights submitted to us provided nothing with regard to the War Measures Act, that is, with regard to that troubled period where a bill of rights and fundamental freedoms is so

much needed; and in the fifth instance, I seriously criticized the government for presenting this legislation when the session is drawing to a close.
I shall now elaborate on each of those points with regard to the amendments now submitted today.
The scope of the bill, even with the amendments to which we contributed, is still much too limited. I think it is very unfortunate that certain people should have tried to exaggerate its importance because I am absolutely convinced that, when the bill is passed, it will give rise to much confusion and disappointment.
I shall give a few instances in which the bill does not take care of the requirements of Canadian life in 1960. First of all, it is written, right in the preamble, that the bill is limited to the legislative jurisdiction of the Canadian parliament. Therefore, if after this bill is passed by this house and by the Senate and has become law, a coloured person in any province is refused admission to a hotel on account of his colour, this bill will be of no help at all, because Bill C-79 has no provisions on the basis of which corrective action could be taken against racial discrimination.
Second, if this bill comes into force tomorrow and the very next day, close to Ottawa, as happened recently, a witness called before some organization is refused the services of an interpreter, thus preventing that person from giving evidence in his mother tongue, then Bill C-79 could not correct such an unpleasant situation, although that witness would obviously not have received a fair treatment.
I shall give another example with regard to freedom of religion.
Should this bill be passed tomorrow, the next day it might be decreed, as happened a few days ago in Quebec, if I remember correctly, in the case of the Quebec attorney general v. Laurier Saumure, that the matter is a provincial responsibility as decided by Hon. Justice Lizotte.
Those, Mr. Chairman, are three cases which have arisen within a few days and for which this Bill C-79 offers no remedy.
I shall even go a little farther. When the bill was introduced and discussed on July 1, hon. members will recall that it contained no reference to the word "family".
Not once in the bill placed before us by the Prime Minister on July 1 can we find the word "family".

Mr. Chairman, if you will allow me one moment to complete my explanation, I shall be brief.
The family, which is the cornerstone of our society, was not even mentioned in the bill laid before us by the Prime Minister on July 1. Later, we took up the bill in committee, and now-this is in reply to my hon. friend from St. Mary (Mr. Valade)-we find the word "family" in the preamble, but the preamble does not provide any rights for the family.
Mr. Chairman, before we call it eleven o'clock, I would ask the hon. member who interjected a moment ago to try to find, in the bill as amended today, a safeguard and a protection for the Canadian family which, I repeat, is the cornerstone of our society.

Mr. Speaker, we shall continue tomorrow with Bill No. C-79 an act for the recognition and protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. On Wednesday we shall commence with the estimates of the Department of National Defence, and I am suggesting a change in the order of estimates for this week. The next department will be trade and commerce followed by finance followed by the privy council.
As this is Monday, the house might like to know what further business may be before it, and I might list the items now. We have for consideration at any time which becomes available during the course of the week the second reading of Bill No. C-89, an act to amend the Judges Act; concurrence in the report of the civil service commission concerning the House of Commons staff, and the report of the committee on procedure.
